articles.title: Abundance Redistribution Increases Predator‐Prey Interaction Potentials Among North American Birds
articles.titleEn: Abundance Redistribution Increases Predator‐Prey Interaction Potentials Among North American Birds
articles.abstract: Species are shifting their geographical ranges, yet the consequences of these spatial redistributions for species interactions have not been examined at broad spatial and temporal scales. Here, we characterize shifts in the potential for predator‐prey interactions among North American birds over the past 50 years. We first predict potential predator‐prey interactions based on existing data, then construct a novel, abundance‐weighted metric of interaction potential for each pair of predator and prey species in local communities. We found nearly universal increases in predator‐prey interaction potentials across North America that are mostly driven by increases in predator abundances. The spatial redistributions of predators and prey lead to turnover of interactions within local communities that are less associated with changes in climate than with human‐induced land use changes. Our results highlight the importance of considering traits, abundances, and species interactions—including known and potential interactions—when studying the ecological consequences of range shifts.

articles.title: Phenology and surface energy balance changes across northern lands
articles.titleEn: Phenology and surface energy balance changes across northern lands
articles.abstract: Plant phenological shifts – notably earlier start (SOS) and later end (EOS) of the growing season – affect surface albedo, latent and sensible heat fluxes, and ultimately the surface temperature. The magnitude and spatial variability of these effects remain uncertain. Using Earth observation and reanalysis data (2001–2021), we quantify the sensitivity of surface energy fluxes to SOS and EOS changes across northern lands (> 30° N), and we report uncertainties and convergence across multiple independent datasets. Spatially-aggregated results show that an earlier SOS is generally associated with decreased albedo by up to 0.003 d −1 (needleleaf forests and tundra), and increased latent heat fluxes by 0.47 Wm-2d-1 (spatial median), ranging from 0.15 Wm-2d-1 (croplands) to 0.68 Wm-2d-1 (mixed forests). Delays in EOS are also associated with decreases in albedo, though much smaller in magnitude, and with increases in latent heat flux – up to ∼0.14 Wm-2d-1 in mixed forests – with weaker and more variable responses across other land-cover types. Datasets reveal large spatial variability and discrepancies in the responses of the sensible heat fluxes and thus evaporative fraction. Across datasets, earlier SOS is consistently associated with increased latent heat flux, and the concurrent evidence from evaporative fraction suggests a shift towards enhanced latent cooling. These findings are consistent with a phenology-driven negative feedback on surface warming through enhanced evaporative cooling, although causal attribution from observational analyses alone is not possible.

articles.title: Field surveying and numerical simulation of the Typhoon Hato storm surge event in Guangdong province, China
articles.titleEn: Field surveying and numerical simulation of the Typhoon Hato storm surge event in Guangdong province, China
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: In 2017, Typhoon Hato hitting Zhuhai city, Guangdong province, caused a severe storm surge disaster. In this study, a systematic field survey of the “Hato” storm surge was conducted and the numerical modeling of inundation extent and depth was performed. The survey integrated floating debris tracking, inundation tracing, and local inquiries to determine the seawater inundation edge points, water depths, and overall extent of the flooding. articles.title: Persistence of scour at bridges using stochastic simulations
articles.titleEn: Persistence of scour at bridges using stochastic simulations
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: The stochastic and deterministic properties of the scouring process at bridges are analysed by coupling synthetic streamflow generations with a scour and fill model considering the upstream sediment supply. Streamflow was generated using the asymmetric moving-average (AMA) scheme that preserves the Hurst-Kolmogorov (HK) dynamics, the second-order dependence structure, time asymmetry, and the first four statistical moments of the marginal distribution. Stationarity, homogeneity, and ergodicity of the streamflow and scouring processes were assumed. Monte Carlo analyses covered 12 000 realisations for each of the three considered scenarios with different upstream sediment supply. Extreme scour events were assessed using annual maxima with GEV fitting and compared against the equilibrium scour. The dependence structure was identified with the climacogram and climacospectrum stochastic tools and fitted with a filtered HK model (FHK-CD). The obtained results show a multi-scale dynamics of the scouring process with rough and weak persistent behaviour ( M ≈0.40; H ≈0.60), while envelopes span from antipersistent to strongly persistent scour regimes ( H up to ≈0.86) depending on the upstream sediment supply. It is worth noting that the upstream sediment supply reduced the envelope variability and modified the extreme scour values. Additionally, synchronisation between extreme events of streamflow and scour showed a weak correspondence (Critical Success Index ≈0.15–0.60), indicating that streamflow extremes do not systematically translate into scour extremes. Finally, scour depths with a given return period (computed from scour time series) increase with upstream sediment supply.

articles.title: Multi-scale dynamics and mesoscale drivers of the catastrophic September 2022 Marche (central Italy) flood
articles.titleEn: Multi-scale dynamics and mesoscale drivers of the catastrophic September 2022 Marche (central Italy) flood
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: The catastrophic flood that hit the Marche region (central Italy) on 15 September 2022 has been analyzed using high-resolution Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations. The convective rainfall event responsible for the flood was favored by the passage of warm, moist air masses that interacted with the central Apennines. The convective cells, triggered by the rough orography of the area, formed quasi-stationary bands that caused high rainfall accumulation in limited areas. The formation of these rainbands was sustained by the interaction between the low-level flow and the local topography, which generated a persistent low-level convergence line extending downwind from Mount Amiata northeastward towards the Apennines. The observed vertical profile upstream of the orography reveals that the instability was initially suppressed by an inversion layer and was released only when the humid air arrived at low levels and eroded the inhibition. Furthermore, the simulations suggest that gravity waves induced by the mountains may have helped to sustain the vertical motion of the impinging air, and highlight the role of upper-level dynamics (passage of a jet streak). The comparison with surface stations shows that the simulation underestimates peak accumulations (160–180 mm simulated vs. over 400 mm observed), delays the event by 1–2 h, and misses the final phase. However, overall the model captures the system's spatial position, orientation, and quasi-stationary evolution associated with orographic anchoring. Rather than evaluating predictive skill in an operational-like perspective, this study investigates the physical precursors and dynamical mechanisms of the event. Sensitivity experiments reveal a strong dependence on initial and boundary conditions. A comparison of the control run (forced with Global Data Assimilation System (GDAS) analysis/forecasts) with a simulation driven by European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) analysis/forecasts shows a strong sensitivity to the low-level dynamics. Although the large-scale upper-level forcing is almost identical, the ECMWF-driven forecast fails to reproduce the correct amount and distribution of rainfall due to a weaker surface pressure gradient, reduced moisture advection, and lower instability at the time of the event. Specifically, the simulation forced with the ECMWF data anticipates the arrival of the moist air mass, determining a timing mismatch between the low-level supply of moist air (and the consequent release of instability) and the upper-level forcing. This lack of synchronization shifts the rainfall away from the observed area.

articles.title: GATA transcription factors coordinate developmental progression in the arabidopsis root
articles.titleEn: GATA transcription factors coordinate developmental progression in the arabidopsis root
articles.abstract: Proper organ development requires the coordination of cell type-specific differentiation programs with general maturation processes through precise spatiotemporal gene regulation. In plants, where RNA polymerase pausing is not well established, alternative mechanisms must ensure this coordination. Here, using single-cell resolution transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility data, we reconstruct developmental trajectories of the Arabidopsis root ground tissue to investigate these mechanisms. We describe phased transcriptional landscapes governing the transition from stem cell to early differentiation, in which chromatin accessibility marks the activation of key developmental regulators. A major transcriptional switch in the late meristematic zone, underpinned by extensive chromatin remodeling, drives the transition from cell division to differentiation. Leveraging machine learning to examine integrated transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility trajectories, we identify GATA transcription factors (TFs) as central coordinators of this switch; a role we validate experimentally. We show that the GATA TFs sit at the tipping point of a feedback-driven bistable system that integrates inputs from auxin and cytokinin to balance proliferation and differentiation, ensuring temporal precision in root development at both the tissue and organ scales.

articles.title: A geospatial approach to measuring economic activity
articles.titleEn: A geospatial approach to measuring economic activity
articles.abstract: We introduce a methodology to detect and measure economic activity using geospatial data and apply it to steel production, a major industrial pollution source worldwide. Combining plant output data with geospatial data, such as ambient air pollutants, nighttime lights, and temperature, we train machine learning models to predict plant locations and output. We identify about 88% (94%) of plants missing from the training sample within a 1 km (5 km) radius and achieve R 2 above 0.8 for output prediction at a 1 km grid and at the plant level, as well as both regional and time series validations. We use the model trained on Chinese steel data to reliably detect the location and measure the total annual output of steel plants in South Korea and Iran. Our approach can be adapted to other industries and regions, and used by policymakers and researchers to track and measure industrial activity in near real time.

articles.title: Overconsumption of low-digestible sugars can increase susceptibility to Salmonella Typhimurium infection
articles.titleEn: Overconsumption of low-digestible sugars can increase susceptibility to Salmonella Typhimurium infection
articles.abstract: Low-digestible carbohydrates (LDCs), including dietary fibers and sugars that resist absorption, are generally considered beneficial for the gut microbiota. However, we show that acute overconsumption of certain LDCs, particularly low-digestible sugars (LDSs), such as arabinose, lactulose, and polyols commonly used as sugar substitutes, can compromise colonization resistance against the common foodborne pathogen Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium. LDS overconsumption results in elevated fecal pathogen loads, systemic dissemination, and colitis in infected mice. Mechanistic analysis of arabinose overconsumption revealed that rapid fermentation acidifies the intestinal environment, perturbs the microbiota, alters gut-luminal short-chain fatty acid levels and elevated amino acid availability, which can support pathogen growth. Additionally, this perturbation impacts virulence by broadening tissue tropism (e.g. expansion to small intestine) and selecting for invasive Salmonella . Unlike antibiotic perturbations, Salmonella colonization requires SPI-1 and SPI-2 Type-III-secretion systems, linking virulence to pathogen fitness. These findings reveal how dietary perturbations can impact the gut ecosystem in ways that not only compromise colonization resistance but also enhance pathogen virulence.

articles.title: Technical note: Evaluation of snow water equivalent from large-scale land-surface products over Italy
articles.titleEn: Technical note: Evaluation of snow water equivalent from large-scale land-surface products over Italy
articles.abstract: Snow water equivalent (SWE) is a critical hydrological variable for water resource management in mountainous regions, where seasonal snowpacks function as natural reservoirs regulating streamflow and water supply. While high-resolution, observation-constrained regional or national snow products provide reliable daily SWE estimates at fine spatial resolution (less than 1 km), their limited temporal coverage often restricts their use for long-term hydro-climatological studies. Large-scale land-surface products, in which SWE is derived from land-surface model simulations driven by atmospheric reanalyses or regional dynamical downscaling systems, provide multi-decadal coverage, but their reliability may be affected by biases in meteorological forcing, limited topographic representation, and simplified snow process parameterisation, requiring rigorous regional evaluation. This study evaluates the SWE estimates of three large-scale land-surface products, i.e., the global ERA5-Land, the European CERRA-Land, and the Italian VHR-REA_IT, against the national reference dataset IT-SNOW across Italy. The analysis combines grid-scale bias assessment of mean annual SWE and snow cover duration with temporal correlation analysis of daily SWE series, and is complemented by an evaluation of precipitation and temperature biases in each product, providing insight into how each product represents the atmospheric conditions governing snow accumulation and ablation and thereby supporting the interpretation of the identified SWE discrepancies. The results show clear regional differences in product performance, with no single product performing best across all metrics. ERA5-Land shows the strongest temporal correlation with IT-SNOW, but tends to overestimate mean annual SWE and snow cover duration in the Alps. CERRA-Land shows more moderate biases than ERA5-Land in the Italian Alps, but generally underestimates mean annual SWE across most subregions, where autumn and winter precipitation deficits in the forcing limit snow accumulation. Across the Apennines, both ERA5-Land and CERRA-Land tend to underestimate SWE and snow cover duration, particularly in the northern sectors. VHR-REA_IT shows widespread underestimation and the weakest temporal correspondence with IT-SNOW despite its finer grid spacing, which may be due to its fully coupled atmosphere–land architecture with no assimilation of meteorological observations. Overall, the results suggest that forcing biases explain a substantial part of the observed SWE discrepancies, although not all of them. This study provides useful insights for the use of SWE estimates from large-scale land-surface products in long-term hydro-climatological assessments over Italy and helps to understand whether the products can be used to evaluate snow dynamics in mountainous regions lacking high-quality benchmark estimates.

articles.title: Technical note: Benefits of Bayesian estimation of model parameters in a large hydrological model ensemble
articles.titleEn: Technical note: Benefits of Bayesian estimation of model parameters in a large hydrological model ensemble
articles.abstract: Quantifying and mitigating parametric and structural uncertainties in hydrological models are crucial to accurately understand and predict the rainfall-runoff process. Despite recent advances in Bayesian approaches for quantifying structural uncertainty using very large hydrological model ensembles, the simultaneous quantification of both parametric and structural uncertainties has yet to be implemented since previous works on large model ensembles have relied on deterministic optimization of parameters. Here we present the potential benefits of Bayesian estimation of parametric uncertainty within a large hydrological model ensemble. We find that Bayesian estimation of model parameters (more generally, change in calibration methods) potentially influences the interpretation of model comparisons. Specifically, Bayesian parametric uncertainty quantification greatly benefits complex models with many parameters, thereby affecting discussions of the appropriate level of model complexity. We also find that Bayesian parametric uncertainty quantification does not substantially improve multi-model hydrological predictions. The adverse effects of parameter misspecification in individual models are effectively mitigated by combining models with diverse structures. Thus, the high computational cost of Bayesian parameter estimation is not paid for to improve rainfall-runoff analysis in a large hydrological model ensemble.

articles.title: HESS Opinions: Operationalizing sociohydrology from systems thinking to systems doing for sustainable and resilient water management
articles.titleEn: HESS Opinions: Operationalizing sociohydrology from systems thinking to systems doing for sustainable and resilient water management
articles.abstract: Sociohydrology has advanced explanations of coupled human-water systems, but its translation into decision support remains uneven. We propose two complementary approaches to move from systems thinking to systems doing: (i) canonical feedback structures, which describe the main components of human-water systems and how they interact and enable comparison across cases while accounting for important local differences; and (ii) critical pathways, which trace how management actions propagate through these components to produce outcomes, including unintended consequences. Drawing on cases such as the levee effect and reservoir effect, these approaches connect system understanding with intervention design, monitoring, and adaptive learning. We then propose a minimal “systems-doing loop” that links the decision setting, feedback mapping, pathway tracing, indicator selection, and iteration, with equity and legitimacy treated as explicit constraints on useful knowledge and acceptable action. This framing complements predictive modelling and integrated water resources management by accounting for potential unintended consequences in decision-making and clarifying what to monitor and revisit as systems change.

articles.title: Role of hydrometeorological variables and catchment area to flood generation over the monsoonal climate region of India
articles.titleEn: Role of hydrometeorological variables and catchment area to flood generation over the monsoonal climate region of India
articles.abstract: Indian River basins experience frequent flooding during the Indian summer monsoon and pose several challenges for the region's large population, yet the hydrometeorological and catchment-scale drivers that control flood processes remain poorly explored across India. To effectively manage flood risk in the densely populated Indian region, it is essential to understand how the temporal properties of precipitation and runoff generate floods across different aridity regimes within a large catchment, and which specific areas of a large, climatically heterogeneous basin generate the runoff that drives downstream flood peaks. In this study, we address these gaps and examine the role of hydrometeorological variables (such as precipitation and surface runoff) and catchment area in the flood occurrence in the Godavari River basin (one of the largest river basins in the Indian Subcontinent) using observed and VIC-simulated datasets. Based on the temporal analysis of precipitation, runoff, and streamflow, we show that the majority of floods in the semi-humid sub-basins (Tekra, Pathagudam, Perur, and Polavaram) are predominantly associated with 10 to 11 d of accumulated precipitation, having multiple high-intensity precipitation events prior to flood. In contrast, the floods in the semi-arid region of Godavari (Mancherial sub-basin) are triggered by a single high-intensity precipitation day and are associated with short-duration (2 d) accumulated precipitation. In addition to temporal analysis, we performed Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) analysis using precipitation, runoff, and streamflow data to identify the specific sub-regions that disproportionately generate flood-causing runoff (flood-dominant catchment areas). Our results demonstrate that central and downstream areas of the basin contribute dominantly to flood occurrence, generating substantially higher runoff in the Tekra sub-basin. Overall, this study moves beyond basin-averaged flood attribution and advances understanding of flood-generating mechanisms over the Godavari River basin, which can be helpful for duration-informed forecasting and catchment-scale flood management during the monsoonal climate of the Indian Subcontinent.

articles.title: MLAWind: a monthly sea surface wind dataset derived from an interpretable machine learning approach integrating in-situ observations and satellite data
articles.titleEn: MLAWind: a monthly sea surface wind dataset derived from an interpretable machine learning approach integrating in-situ observations and satellite data
articles.abstract: A gridded sea surface wind dataset with long temporal coverage is crucial for understanding atmospheric circulation changes and air–sea interactions at different time scales. This study employs an interpretable machine learning model based on random forest algorithm to generate a 1° × 1° monthly sea surface wind dataset (MLAWind) from 1950 to 2023, covering the near-global ocean within 60° S–60° N. The data reconstruction model integrates the Cross-Calibrated Multi-Platform (CCMP) satellite data and the spatially sparse long-term International Comprehensive Ocean-Atmosphere Data Set (ICOADS), exhibiting robust interpretability and generalization capability. Quantitative validations against satellite and in-situ data indicate that MLAWind achieves better consistency with observations than most reanalysis datasets, maintaining robust performance during both training (1993–2022) and testing periods (2023). The performance of MLAWind since 1950 is assessed across multiple time scales. Its characteristics in climatology, annual cycle, and inter-annual variability are comparable to those of reanalysis datasets, even during the non-satellite period prior to 1993. Independent coral records from 1950–1982 are employed as proxy indicators to evaluate long-term sea surface wind trends. The trend derived from MLAWind is corroborated by these proxies, exhibiting significantly higher temporal correlation than those obtained from reanalysis products. MLAWind demonstrates a more reliable reconstruction of long-term sea surface wind variability during historical periods since 1950. The results indicate that MLAWind serves as a robust data resource for global climate change research. The reconstructed MLAWind dataset is publicly accessible at https://doi.org/10.12157/IOCAS.20250707.001 (Guo et al., 2025c).

articles.title: Network-based subbasin-scale mapping of streamflow alteration in Ontario, Canada
articles.titleEn: Network-based subbasin-scale mapping of streamflow alteration in Ontario, Canada
articles.abstract: Dams, reservoirs, waterpower facilities, and other water-control structures can modify streamflow and propagate their influence downstream through connected river networks, complicating hydrologic modelling and aquatic ecosystem assessment. Large-domain assessments often rely on binary agency classifications at hydrometric gauges (e.g., “natural” and “regulated”) or on storage- and discharge-based metrics that are difficult to apply consistently where operational data are incomplete. We introduce the Streamflow Alteration Index (SAI), a parsimonious, network-based screening metric that estimates the percentage of upstream drainage area whose routed flow passes through mapped alteration signal sources. Under a first-order drainage-area scaling approximation, SAI provides a proxy for the fraction of streamflow potentially exposed to upstream alteration sources, rather than a measure of the exact magnitude of hydrologic alteration. The framework comprises two paired indices, SAI_I (0 %–100 %) and SAI_II (0 %–100 %), independently representing confirmed Level I and potential Level II sources; values are propagated downstream by drainage-area-weighted mixing and reset at new sources of the same level. We compiled 2528 infrastructure records, of which 2476 were retained after geospatial alignment and screening. Following source classification and consolidation of multiple records within the same subbasin, 643 unique subbasins were identified as Level I and/or Level II alteration signal locations. The resulting SAI v1.0 database provides province-wide subbasin and river-reach layers for screening potential instream alteration at gauged and ungauged locations. We evaluated SAI-derived natural, conditional, and altered classes against 148 Reference Hydrometric Basin Network (RHBN) gauges, 125 additional Water Survey of Canada (WSC) gauges labelled natural, and 215 WSC-regulated gauges. SAI classified 86 % of both natural reference groups as natural, with no RHBN gauge classified as altered. Among WSC-regulated gauges, 26 % were classified as altered, 40 % as conditional, and 34 % as natural, highlighting differences between binary agency labels and the SAI screening framework and identifying sites requiring follow-up assessment. SAI v1.0 therefore provides a practical, transparent, and reproducible screening baseline for large-domain hydrologic and ecological applications without requiring detailed operating rules and offers a scalable framework for broader network-based assessments of potential streamflow alteration. The SAI v1.0 dataset is available from Zenodo (Shen et al., 2026; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19547932).

articles.title: Ten years of measurements (2012-2022) of the atmospheric composition at Saclay/SIRTA observatory in the Ile de France region as part of ICOS and ACTRIS
articles.titleEn: Ten years of measurements (2012-2022) of the atmospheric composition at Saclay/SIRTA observatory in the Ile de France region as part of ICOS and ACTRIS
articles.abstract: Carbon dioxide (CO 2 )is the main contributor to global warming, and cities now account for more than two-thirds of emissions of this gas. Atmospheric observatories located on the outskirts of cities are therefore important facilities for measuring the impact on atmospheric composition of the emission reductions planned by cities. The Saclay observatory, part of the ICOS and ACTRIS research infrastructures and located 20 km southwest of Paris, has been monitoring greenhouse gases (CO 2 , methane – CH 4 ), reactive gases (Nitrogen oxides – NO x , Ozone – O 3 , Carbon monoxide – CO), and carbonaceous aerosols (eBC) since 2012 (https://doi.org/10.57932/5c399263-a317-41b7-8900-184b177c4216, Bouillon and Ramonet, 2025). This study presents 10 years of monitoring of these compounds, characterizing diurnal, seasonal cycles and decadal trends. In order to best characterize the impact of Parisian emissions, we defined two sets of data depending on whether the station is downwind of Paris or, conversely, in background conditions with westerly winds. This strategy allows us to characterize the urban offset in the Saclay measurement series. The results show a significant decrease in the urban offset of compounds mainly linked to traffic emissions: −35.6 %, −52.3 %, and −56.7 % for CO, NO x , and eBC lf (equivalent black carbon from liquid fuel). There was also a 15 % decrease in urban offset of CO 2 between the 2012–2017 and 2019–2022 periods, a figure consistent with the Airparif inventories' estimate of the decrease in emissions in Paris over the same period.

articles.title: Plant‐ and Microbial‐Derived Soil Organic Carbon: Global Patterns and Divergent Climatic Associations
articles.titleEn: Plant‐ and Microbial‐Derived Soil Organic Carbon: Global Patterns and Divergent Climatic Associations
articles.abstract: Soil organic carbon (SOC) pools reflect the net balance of plant‐ and microbial‐derived inputs, transformation, and loss, yet a global‐scale assessment of distribution patterns, relative contributions, and hierarchical environmental correlates of microbial necromass carbon (MNC) and plant‐derived carbon (PdC) remains incomplete. Based on 1167 site‐level observations (1235 pool‐level records) across four ecosystem types, we applied variance partitioning, random forest, linear mixed‐effects models, and structural equation modeling to quantify global patterns and associative pathways of the two carbon pools. Unadjusted pooled comparisons showed higher MNC concentration and SOC contribution than PdC. However, covariate‐adjusted linear mixed‐effects models revealed significantly higher PdC. Paired observations showed the same directional trend, although statistical significance was not reached due to limited paired sample size (concentration: p = 0.104; contribution: p = 0.140). The apparent MNC dominance constitutes a Simpson's paradox driven by uneven ecosystem sampling, rather than a consistent within‐ecosystem pattern. Instead, the relative contribution of MNC and PdC was ecosystem‐dependent: MNC was marginally higher in forests, whereas PdC dominated in croplands and wetlands, with no significant difference in grasslands in paired observations. Edaphic variables were the strongest predictors (independent explanatory power: 61.1% for MNC, 47.4% for PdC), with total nitrogen, C:N ratio, pH, and mean annual temperature as key correlates. Our results reveal a hierarchical associative cascade in which geographic factors covary with climate, which in turn correlates with edaphic properties as the strongest direct predictors. Climate shows a weak but significant negative direct association with MNC only. This synthesis provides a hierarchical correlative framework and biome‐specific baseline parameters to support explicit representation of plant‐ and microbial‐mediated SOC pathways in Earth system models.

articles.title: Intensification and Spatial Reorganization of Drought Risks for Global Rainfed Crops Under Climate Change
articles.titleEn: Intensification and Spatial Reorganization of Drought Risks for Global Rainfed Crops Under Climate Change
articles.abstract: Rainfed agriculture covers roughly 80% of global cropland and supplies more than half of global food production, yet uncertainty in how meteorological drying propagates into root‐zone water deficits and crop losses impedes robust risk assessment. Here, we establish an integrated, production‐weighted assessment framework coupling SPEI, SSI, and 12 GGCMI3 crop models to trace how meteorological drying propagates into root‐zone deficits and crop losses, explicitly separating affected area, conditional yield loss, and accumulated production loss across rainfed maize, soybean, and wheat. By 2070–2099, opposing‐direction SPEI–SSI change classes occupied 6.8%–28.4% of rainfed area across crops under SSP1‐2.6/default CO 2 and 26.6%–48.2% under SSP5‐8.5/default CO 2 . Comparison with fixed‐2015 CO 2 experiments (7.5%–27.6% and 21.7%–34.9%, respectively) indicates that elevated CO 2 substantially expanded the spatial footprint of this hydrometeorological decoupling. Historically, SSI‐defined drought affected 12–16 million ha year −1 and was associated with annual production losses of 5–12 Mt year −1 (1.6–2.0% year −1 ). Under default CO 2 , affected area increased to 14–21 million ha under SSP1‐2.6 and 19–27 million ha under SSP5‐8.5, with production losses of 6–12 and 9–12 Mt year −1 , respectively. Under SSP5‐8.5, median loss rates were higher under fixed‐2015 than default CO 2 for maize (3.33 vs. 1.96% year −1 ), soybean (4.22 vs. 2.84% year −1 ) and wheat (5.41 vs. 2.90% year −1 ), as elevated CO 2 reduces stomatal water loss and thus mitigates drought impacts, whereas SSP1‐2.6 estimates were similar. Severe drought became the largest loss contributor under both pathways and CO 2 settings. Under default CO 2 , loss increases clustered in Central America, northeastern Brazil, western Europe and southern Africa; fixed‐2015 CO 2 broadened the area of robust grid‐cell loss increases. These results show that drought‐related production losses are spatially uneven and sensitive to the modeled CO 2 response, highlighting the value of crop‐ and region‐specific risk assessment.

articles.title: Review article: rainfall-induced landslide early warning systems through the lens of the early warnings for all framework – advances, gaps, and perspectives
articles.titleEn: Review article: rainfall-induced landslide early warning systems through the lens of the early warnings for all framework – advances, gaps, and perspectives
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: This review is necessary to provide a comprehensive evaluation of rainfall-induced landslide early warning systems (LEWS) through the lens of the United Nations “Early Warnings for All” (EW4All) framework. This study integrates EW4All pillars, examines information sharing in academic publications and official websites/portals, and evaluates the global feasibility of implementing EW4All for LEWS. Of 45 rainfall-induced systems, 27 (26 LEWS and one forecasting-focused system) were found operational (benefiting 19 countries), meaning they were implemented and actively used for warning purposes when this paper was prepared. Some forecasting-focused systems were misleadingly described as early warning systems. Among Local, Regional and National systems, Local systems were often less scalable and more resource-intensive. Operational systems were mainly National, followed by Regional. Most operational systems relied on rainfall thresholds. Some included susceptibility maps; risk maps were largely absent. Real-time sensor data were used in some systems; however, high maintenance costs limited scalability. Reliability was further constrained by data scarcity, limited forecast verification, and suboptimal use of Artificial Intelligence. Community engagement was infrequently documented in the reviewed systems. Although EW4All is transformative, implementing effective LEWS across rainfall-induced landslide-prone areas worldwide by 2027 remains impractical without localised approaches, sufficient funding, community engagement, and enhanced institutional capacity.

articles.title: Unravelling information on impactful geo-hydrological hazard events with HazMiner, a multilingual text mining method developed through a global scale coverage application
articles.titleEn: Unravelling information on impactful geo-hydrological hazard events with HazMiner, a multilingual text mining method developed through a global scale coverage application
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: The incidence and impacts of geo-hydrological hazards such as floods, flash floods and landslides are changing globally due to anthropogenic environmental changes and increased exposure driven by population growth. Reliable datasets on geo-hydrological hazards are essential to deepen our understanding of these hazards and their impacts. However, existing geo-hydrological hazard datasets contain data gaps leading to biased interpretations, especially in low- and lower-middle-income countries where populations are commonly the most impacted. Text mining offers new opportunities in documenting geo-hydrological hazards by automatically extracting information from large text corpora. Despite its potential, current methodologies are not adapted to improve documentation in data-scarce contexts. We introduce HazMiner, a paragraph-based text mining method designed to document the location, timing and impact of geo-hydrological hazards through transformer-based natural language processing models across multiple languages and at various scales. Applied here globally on 6 366 905 news articles published from 2017 through 2024 in 58 languages, HazMiner extracted 15 313 flood, 6836 landslide and 2258 flash flood events with a known location and time information and, in some cases, impact data. Compared to existing hazard datasets, HazMiner significantly improved hazard documentation, reducing the data gaps in many regions, especially in low- and lower-middle-income countries. This new versatile multilingual method and its dataset advance the accessibility and use of text mined natural hazard data.

articles.title: Reducing false alarms in crackmeter-based early warning of small-scale slope deformation via deep learning-driven asynchronous displacement–rainfall data fusion
articles.titleEn: Reducing false alarms in crackmeter-based early warning of small-scale slope deformation via deep learning-driven asynchronous displacement–rainfall data fusion
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Real-time crackmeter-based deformation monitoring systems for small-scale rainfall-affected slopes suffer from high false alarm rates. Across multi-slope monitoring settings, threshold-based alerts are vulnerable to noise, while conventional denoising and prediction-based validation methods remain limited in automated warning discrimination and cross-site generalization. To address this bottleneck, a labeled dataset and a data-driven binary classification framework were developed to distinguish true early warnings from false alarms among threshold-triggered sensor alerts. A multi-source dataset of crack-displacement and rainfall observations was constructed from monitored slopes in Fujian Province, China, with genuine and false alerts labelled based on field investigations and geological expert assessment. A patch-based dual-branch temporally-aware Transformer model was developed to fuse asynchronous multi-rate data, preserve the temporal direction from antecedent rainfall to subsequent displacement, and satisfy stringent real-time decision constraints. By simultaneously capturing long-term rainfall-displacement interactions and high-resolution displacement dynamics, the model outperforms competitive baselines, achieving a precision of 90.32 %, a recall of 89.38 %, and an F 2 -score of 89.54 % in identifying true early warnings. Interpretability analysis reveals that the model's decisions are primarily driven by localized displacement trends and the relationship between rainfall and displacement, aligning with expert judgment. Analyses of misclassified cases informed additional safeguards to further reduce missed warnings. The proposed framework helps reduce false alarms and supports reliable automated slope hazard monitoring. However, the present validation is limited to the Fujian rainfall-triggered monitoring context, and application to other geological or climatic settings requires further external validation and local adaptation.

articles.title: Microclimate, Vegetation, and Soil Response to Micro‐Zonal Solar Photovoltaic Patterning in a Humid Sub‐Tropical Agrivoltaic Grazing System
articles.titleEn: Microclimate, Vegetation, and Soil Response to Micro‐Zonal Solar Photovoltaic Patterning in a Humid Sub‐Tropical Agrivoltaic Grazing System
articles.abstract: Agrivoltaic grazing systems, or the integration of solar photovoltaic (PV) energy generation with livestock grazing, are the most common form of multi‐use solar energy in the United States and much of the world. However, there is a substantial gap in our understanding of the ecological impacts of combining PV and grazing in these novel ecosystems. Addressing this gap, we present data from the first 2 years of a study characterizing the interacting effects of PV infrastructure with land management (sheep grazing and mowing) in the Southeastern US. We observed spatial and temporal solar radiation and precipitation patterning among micro‐zones unique to the humid‐subtropical climate region and found that the PV modules maintained higher soil moisture than in the absence of PV, across all micro‐zones, with more dramatic differences observed during drier periods. Despite the significant patterning of microclimate conditions, we found no significant difference in above‐ground primary productivity across any micro‐zones or between management treatments within the array. Three years after construction, we detected no significant difference in soil carbon stocks across micro‐zones.

articles.title: Manhattan Pluvial Flood Simulations Under Two Extreme Rainfall Scenarios Show Similar Severity Patterns but Contrasting Peak Timing Across Districts
articles.titleEn: Manhattan Pluvial Flood Simulations Under Two Extreme Rainfall Scenarios Show Similar Severity Patterns but Contrasting Peak Timing Across Districts
articles.abstract: Urban pluvial flooding is often summarized by peak depth, peak extent, or cumulative burden, but these metrics do not distinguish when flooding first becomes hazardous from when the hazardous area becomes largest. This study introduces an activation–occupancy framework to quantify these two times and applies it to building‐resolving shallow‐water simulations of Manhattan ( at m resolution) under an Ida‐derived hyetograph and New York City's 1‐hr design storm. Under the Ida‐derived rainfall at the 0.3‐m threshold, district activation peaks occur within a 35‐min span, whereas the times of maximum hazard extent are much more dispersed. Under the shorter design storm, peak timing compresses sharply. Rainfall is spatially uniform in both simulations, so the 35‐min activation spread reflects routing alone and provides a lower bound on the variability of activation timing; spatial rainfall heterogeneity lies outside the modeled scenarios. Across the two modeled rainfall scenarios, severe‐flooding geography remains broadly consistent: the same seven districts exceed the borough reference at 0.2, 0.3, and 0.4 m, with the strongest rank preservation for eventual extent and hazardous area–time burden. At 0.5 m, that set contracts to six because Lower East Side/Chinatown falls just below the borough reference in both scenarios. East Harlem remains the principal exception in design‐storm timing at the deeper thresholds. These diagnostics distinguish severity patterns relevant to adaptation from scenario‐specific timing information for warning and response.

articles.title: Temperature Carryover Effect Revealed for Marine Fishes Using Spatio‐Temporal Distributed Lag Models
articles.titleEn: Temperature Carryover Effect Revealed for Marine Fishes Using Spatio‐Temporal Distributed Lag Models
articles.abstract: Understanding the impact of changing temperature on population densities is necessary to predict the likely impact of climate anomalies (e.g., marine heatwaves) or forecast distribution shifts under future climate scenarios. Population densities are often analyzed using spatio‐temporal models (STMs), which typically predict densities based on local habitat conditions while also estimating latent spatial and spatio‐temporal variation. Recent research extends STMs by also estimating density responses to habitat conditions at nearby locations using a “spatially distributed lag” (SDL) that averages habitat conditions in the vicinity of samples. Here, we extend the SDL by incorporating insights from diffusion‐enhanced STMs to simultaneously estimate spatially distributed and time‐lagged responses to nearby and past habitat conditions (a “spatio‐temporal distributed lag” STDL). We then use summer bottom trawl survey data from the eastern Bering Sea (1982–2024) to measure whether spatial and/or temporal lags are parsimonious when predicting population density from temperature anomalies for six ecologically important fishes. Results show that time‐lagged responses are parsimonious, positive, and substantial (correlation of 0.20–0.83 per year) for five species, and that density responses to temperature anomalies also diffuse outward over time for four species at 30–53 km per year. A self‐ and cross‐test simulation experiment shows that model selection can identify the appropriate model and that parameter estimates are approximately unbiased. We therefore conclude that temperature carryover effects arise in marine fishes and implement the method in the R package sdmTMB so that future studies can estimate nonlocal and time‐lagged responses when measuring density responses to habitat.

articles.title: Integrating Information From Hydrologic Models and SWOT Remote Sensing Measurements to Estimate Discharge Across River Networks
articles.titleEn: Integrating Information From Hydrologic Models and SWOT Remote Sensing Measurements to Estimate Discharge Across River Networks
articles.abstract: The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) satellite has the potential to improve knowledge of river discharge globally. However, SWOT discharge algorithms are informed by global hydrological model data, and a portion of the model's systematic bias is passed along to the SWOT discharge time series. To address this issue, we present a new algorithm designed to reduce systematic bias in SWOT discharge. The algorithm analytically integrates basin‐scale information by applying mass conservation to time‐averaged SWOT discharge and estimates of regionalized runoff. We test the algorithm on three river basins with drainage areas on the order of 10 5 km 2 . We find that when the time‐averaged SWOT discharge observations are spatially unbiased (i.e., their spatially averaged error is close to zero) the algorithm significantly reduces error in SWOT discharge: the median (interquartile range) absolute value of the normalized error is 15% (10%–19%) for the Willamette River basin, and 12% (7%–48%) for the upper Ohio River basin, significant reduction in SWOT discharge error (median values of 30% and 31%, respectively). However, for the Loire River basin, which has high (∼60%) spatial bias, the algorithm does not reduce error associated with SWOT discharge. These results indicate that understanding and reducing spatial bias at the basin scale is key for reducing time series bias in river discharge. Based on a preliminary assessment of spatial bias globally, we find that SWOT discharge could achieve its target accuracy (30% discharge error, with most of it temporal bias) even in ungaged basins, enabling SWOT discharge to significantly increase accuracies of the global water budget.

articles.title: Coupling MRI and XRCT to Resolve Structure–Transport Evolution During Enzyme‐Induced Calcite Precipitation at the REV Scale
articles.titleEn: Coupling MRI and XRCT to Resolve Structure–Transport Evolution During Enzyme‐Induced Calcite Precipitation at the REV Scale
articles.abstract: The aim of this study is to understand how enzyme‐induced calcite precipitation (EICP) modifies flow and transport in porous media, as this is essential for developing sustainable approaches to soil stabilization, permeability control, and groundwater management. For this, we investigated the coupled evolution of pore structure and hydraulic properties during EICP at the representative elementary volume (REV) scale using a dual non‐invasive imaging approach combining X‐ray computed tomography (XRCT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Three replicate sand columns with initial permeabilities between 22 × 10 −12 m 2 and 25 × 10 −12 m 2 were treated with EICP using a constant flow injection and solutions of 0.5 M CaCl 2 , 0.5 M urea, and 5.0 g L −1 jack bean meal. Over six injection cycles (175 pore volumes), permeability decreased by more than three orders of magnitude, while average porosity declined moderately from 0.38 to 0.28. XRCT revealed that precipitation was concentrated near the inlet, where the surface to volume ratio increased from 0.055 to 0.065 μm −1 and tortuosity rose from ∼2.0 to ∼3.5. MRI measurements showed corresponding localized reductions in water content and relaxation times, with T 1 decreasing from ∼1.5 to ∼1.0 s and T 2 from ∼50 to ∼30 ms. The combined imaging results indicate a two‐stage precipitation process with early pore‐throat blockage followed by progressive narrowing of pore bodies. These findings demonstrate that permeability loss is governed not only by porosity reduction but also by precipitation distribution.

articles.title: Storage, Connectivity, and Stream Drying in Headwater Systems: Modeling Across Hydrogeomorphic Features
articles.titleEn: Storage, Connectivity, and Stream Drying in Headwater Systems: Modeling Across Hydrogeomorphic Features
articles.abstract: Headwater streams play a critical role in the physical, chemical, and biological functions of downstream waters. However, predicting their specific impact on a landscape scale remains a grand challenge, prompting the development of the river corridor framework to integrate the study of stream channels and hyporheic zones with that of adjacent hillslopes and riparian zones. To operationalize this framework and better explore hydrologic fluxes, the intermediate hydrogeomorphic feature (HGF) scale was recently defined to discretize the river corridor into quantifiable and repeatable compartments. In this study, we used process‐based modeling within and across HGFs to evaluate hydrologic connectivity, storage, streamflow, and drying. We used the Advanced Terrestrial Simulator to model hydrologic fluxes in an experimental watershed in the Coastal Plain of the southeastern United States, where we delineated incised, intact riparian, and wetland HGFs along three streams. Among HGFs, incised channels gained the most water from the subsurface, wetland HGFs maintained the highest water tables, and intact riparian HGFs frequently went dry. Incised and wetland HGFs generated the majority of discharge throughout the year, but dry season discharge was dominated by streamflow gains in incised HGFs. Together, these results suggest that stream incision increases downstream connectivity and export, whereas wetland HGFs increase watershed capacity for storage. Our findings highlight the role of geomorphic structure in driving spatial patterns of drying, storage, and connectivity. Given the pervasiveness of stream incision across anthropogenically impacted systems, our results provide a basis for identifying locations significant to watershed‐scale hydrologic export or retention.

articles.title: Hysteretic Dynamics of Stream Network Expansion and Contraction Revealed Through High‐Resolution Integrated Hydrological Modeling
articles.titleEn: Hysteretic Dynamics of Stream Network Expansion and Contraction Revealed Through High‐Resolution Integrated Hydrological Modeling
articles.abstract: As landscapes cycle through wetting and drying, stream networks expand and contract, driving material export and biogeochemical transformations with important implications for water quality and ecosystem function. Because it is challenging to measure the extent of the active network, streamflow () is often used as a proxy. However, the relationship remains uncertain, especially for larger catchments where direct observation is labor intensive. Using a process‐based integrated hydrological model capable of resolving inundation patterns at high spatial and temporal resolution, we study the dynamics of network extent for a 75 km 2 watershed and its subcatchments. Without catchment‐specific calibration, simulations using the ATS integrated hydrology model agree well with observed daily stream discharge and observed stream persistency regime (perennial vs. non‐perennial). Simulation results reveal that a unique, synchronous relationship between and exists only for small catchments. Specifically, the synchronous data exhibit substantial scatter due to hysteresis, which increases with increasing catchment size. However, a robust relationship free of hysteresis emerges when asynchronous event‐scale peaks of and are considered instead. The event‐scale asynchronous relationship is well approximated as power‐law over the range of peak simulated and remains consistent across nested catchments of varying size, independent of antecedent wetness, season, and storm details. In baseflow conditions, the scaling is also well approximated with a power law but with a larger exponent, suggesting different runoff generation mechanisms. These results offer a more robust framework for understanding stream expansion and contraction in larger, more complex basins.

articles.title: Shallow Cumulus Cloud Statistics in Real‐Case Large‐Eddy Simulations and Their Dependence on Soil Moisture
articles.titleEn: Shallow Cumulus Cloud Statistics in Real‐Case Large‐Eddy Simulations and Their Dependence on Soil Moisture
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: The ability of weather and climate models to reproduce the statistical properties of shallow cumulus clouds (SCCs) is critical for representing boundary‐layer transport, cloud cover, and cloud‐radiative effects. This study investigates statistical properties of SCC ensembles using the Icosahedral Nonhydrostatic model in large‐eddy simulation mode for three cases during the Field Experiment on Submesoscale Spatio‐Temporal Variability in Lindenberg campaign. Feature‐based tracking is applied to identify cloud objects and track their evolution. Each cloud is classified as active or passive according to its in‐cloud buoyancy excess. The cloud‐base mass flux distribution of each class is robustly captured by a Weibull distribution. Active clouds exhibit shape parameters , consistent with convective memory related to their life‐cycle, while passive clouds approach , indicating stochastic, short‐lived nature. The bulk cloud‐base mass flux , representing the convective transport of the SCC population, scales linearly with surface heat input per unit cloud moist‐static‐energy excess, weighted by thermodynamic efficiency of the surface‐driven moist heat cycle. This scaling emerges primarily across the soil‐moisture perturbations and holds from moderately moisture‐limited to energy‐limited regimes, but linearity breaks down under very dry conditions, where a suppressed evaporative fraction and the resulting sub‐cloud moisture deficit prevent further increases in . Soil moisture strongly controls cloud number, updraft strength, cloud size, and the mass‐flux distribution, whereas responds to both soil‐moisture perturbations and day‐to‐day large‐scale conditions, highlighting land‐atmosphere coupling as a key regulator of shallow convective variability over land.

articles.title: The true scale of global wildlife trade is obscured by data gaps
articles.titleEn: The true scale of global wildlife trade is obscured by data gaps
articles.abstract: Overexploitation of wildlife is one of the greatest global drivers of biodiversity loss. Yet, despite this well-established risk, data on extraction and trade are both incomplete and highly fragmented. The IPBES Global analysis estimated 50,000 species to be in trade, yet our review of wildlife trade monitoring programs found at least double that, at 107,356 species in use and trade globally. This included up to 47,685 animal species, covering 42% of all described vertebrate species. Most countries lack any systematic data on trade for species not listed in Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), with the exception of the US-specific dataset Law Enforcement Management Information System, which frequently had higher diversity of species in trade than global databases. This highlights the importance of national monitoring efforts and the need for standardized collation of wildlife trade data beyond CITES-listed species. Without these changes, global indicators on trade meant to guide sustainability and conservation will continue to focus on less than 2% of traded species.

articles.title: Atmospheric stabilization of the East Antarctic ice sheet under warming
articles.titleEn: Atmospheric stabilization of the East Antarctic ice sheet under warming
articles.abstract: Most coupled Earth system models do not include fully interactive ice sheets, introducing uncertainty in future projections of polar climate and global sea level. To this end, we conduct 100,000-year-long simulations for different CO 2 conditions using the community Earth system model coupled to the bihemispheric Penn State University ice sheet–ice shelf model. Whereas global warming exceeding 2 °C above pre-industrial conditions and related subsurface ocean warming lead to the millennial-scale disintegration of the West Antarctic ice sheet, the East Antarctic ice sheet shows a much greater resilience, even at 10 °C or more of warming. The simulations reveal that a moister and cloudier atmosphere over Antarctica, with southward-shifted westerlies, increases snow accumulation and reduces shortwave radiation. For Greenland, a 6 °C threshold above pre-industrial levels is identified. Capturing the balance of ocean- and atmosphere-driven ablation and accumulation processes in coupled climate–ice-sheet models will improve projections of long-term sea-level rise.

articles.title: How Water Resource Tax Reform Shapes Corporate Green Investment: Evidence From Financing Capacity and Investment Willingness
articles.titleEn: How Water Resource Tax Reform Shapes Corporate Green Investment: Evidence From Financing Capacity and Investment Willingness
articles.abstract: Water scarcity poses an increasingly severe challenge to sustainable economic development, yet empirical evidence remains limited on how environmental taxation affects corporate green investment (GI) decisions and the micro‐level mechanisms through which these effects operate. Using Chinese A‐share listed firms from 2010 to 2024, this study exploits the 2017 expansion of China's water resource tax reform, a single policy shock varying across regions and industries, and applies a triple‐difference strategy to identify the causal effect of the policy on corporate GI. The results show that water resource tax reform significantly increases corporate GI, and this conclusion remains robust across robustness tests. Mechanism analysis reveals two complementary transmission channels. First, the reform improves firms' green financing capacity by expanding access to debt financing, equity financing, and green credit. Second, firms' willingness to invest in green projects is moderated by managerial characteristics and external environmental regulation. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the policy effect is more pronounced among firms with lower digitalization, higher fixed‐asset intensity, weaker pricing power, and lower market power. Investment‐structure decomposition indicates that the policy effect is concentrated mainly in end‐of‐pipe treatment investment, suggesting that future policy design should provide stronger incentives for preventive GI. Extended analysis further shows that the GI induced by the reform simultaneously increases total factor productivity and reduces water pollution equivalents, supporting the win‐win logic of the Porter hypothesis. These findings provide empirical evidence for improving the design of green fiscal and tax policies.

articles.title: Design and trial implementation of a continental-scale, kilometre-resolution hourly precipitation analysis for Australia using satellite, radar and gauges
articles.titleEn: Design and trial implementation of a continental-scale, kilometre-resolution hourly precipitation analysis for Australia using satellite, radar and gauges
articles.abstract: High-resolution precipitation information is essential for hydrometeorological applications such as extreme weather monitoring, flood forecasting, and disaster risk management. Despite substantial advances in satellite, radar, and gauge observations, producing kilometre-resolution sub-daily precipitation analyses over continental domains remains challenging due to heterogeneous data availability, scale mismatches, and computational constraints. This study presents the design and trial implementation of BRAIN (blended rainfall), a continental-scale, kilometre-resolution hourly precipitation analysis for Australia. In this initial implementation, BRAIN integrates three key data sources from the Australian Bureau of Meteorology: geostationary satellite rainfall estimates (2 km, 10 min) from Himawari, radar rainfall estimates (1 km, 5 min) from the national radar network, and rainfall observations from sub-daily rain gauges. The trialled system incorporates quality control, spatiotemporal aggregation, bias correction, and a simplified statistical interpolation configuration designed to balance analysis performance and computational scalability at the continental scale. Source contributions are weighted according to their spatial and temporal error characteristics, allowing each data type to influence the analysis where it is most informative. articles.title: Deploying machine learning components coupled to Earth System Models with OASIS3-MCT (v6) and Eophis (v1.1)
articles.titleEn: Deploying machine learning components coupled to Earth System Models with OASIS3-MCT (v6) and Eophis (v1.1)
articles.abstract: The integration of machine learning (ML) components into Earth System Models (ESMs) holds significant potential for improving climate simulations, but it is often constrained by challenges related to interoperability, reproducibility, and computational efficiency. This paper presents a novel coupler-based approach that combines the OASIS3-MCT coupling library with Eophis, a high-performance Python library, to seamlessly deploy ML components in ESMs. By leveraging OASIS3-MCT’s robust communication infrastructure, Eophis abstracts the technical complexities of coupling, enabling users to integrate Python-based ML models or analytical parameterizations into geophysical simulations. Eophis provides a modular interface for defining data exchanges, synchronizing time steps, and supporting parallel communications, including advanced features such as halo construction for Convolutional Neural Networks and hybrid CPU/GPU execution. We evaluate this framework by coupling the NEMO4 ocean model with both ML-based and analytical parameterizations, demonstrating scalability, asynchronous execution, and flexible resource allocation. Benchmarking results show that this approach allows for deploying Python scripts in NEMO without affecting time-to-solution, provided extra computing resources are adequately allocated. The combination of OASIS3-MCT and Eophis offers a user-friendly solution for hybrid modelling, which facilitates the integration of ML components into ESM workflows. By lowering the barrier to hybrid modeling, this work facilitates the integration of ML components into ESM workflows. The combination of OASIS3-MCT and Eophis offers a practical solution for bridging the gap between ML and climate modeling, supporting innovation in Earth system science while maintaining reproducibility and ease of use.

articles.title: Towards high-fidelity simulations of coastal submesoscale baroclinic instabilities with MPAS-O (vE3SM3.0.0) – Part 1: Idealized experiments
articles.titleEn: Towards high-fidelity simulations of coastal submesoscale baroclinic instabilities with MPAS-O (vE3SM3.0.0) – Part 1: Idealized experiments
articles.abstract: Rapid advances in computational power over the past decade have enabled global, kilometer-scale simulations that realistically represent open-ocean submesoscale dynamics. However, the ability of global ocean models to represent coastal submesoscale dynamics – where flows are more heterogeneous and strongly shaped by coastlines, bathymetry, and buoyancy inputs – remains largely unexplored. This study is the first of two companion papers comparing coastal submesoscale processes representation in two models with very different numerical approaches: MPAS-O, an unstructured grid global ocean model, and ROMS, a structured grid regional model. This study is the first idealized evaluation of MPAS-O’s representation of coastal submesoscale dynamics using observed conditions in the Mississippi-Atchafalaya (M-A) River plume as a template for initial conditions, with the previously validated ROMS model serving as a benchmark. An important motivation for this study is to examine the suitability of models designed for global ocean simulations in reproducing energetic coastal flows. We compare statistical metrics based on flow invariants – total strain, relative vorticity, and divergence – as well as velocity gradients in frontal coordinates, across horizontal resolutions ranging from 10 km to 100 m within an idealized model domain. We find that the representation of submesoscale baroclinic instabilities is highly similar across all resolutions such that the impact of model choice is smaller than the choice of spatial grid resolution. We also compare numerical and physical mixing between models using online diagnostics based on discrete variance decay. We find that ROMS generally has more numerical mixing and less physical mixing than MPAS-O across all resolutions. Trends in numerical mixing likely arise from MPAS-O's flux-corrected transport tracer advection scheme, which exhibits a stronger variance-producing response relative to the MPDATA scheme used in the ROMS simulations. Trends in physical mixing likely arise from differences in each model’s configuration of the vertical mixing scheme (the K-Profile Parameterization). A companion paper extends this idealized model-model comparison to realistic simulations of the M-A River plume.

articles.title: Nitrous oxide dynamics across nitrogen and pH gradients in headwater streams
articles.titleEn: Nitrous oxide dynamics across nitrogen and pH gradients in headwater streams
articles.abstract: Headwater streams in agricultural landscapes can contribute substantially to nitrous oxide (N 2 O) emissions, yet the environmental controls on stream N 2 O dynamics remain poorly resolved, particularly in systems with low pH. We investigated 72 Danish headwater streams spanning broad gradients in pH (5.0–8.8), land use, and soil type to identify the main drivers of N 2 O variability. Nitrate (NO3-) was the strongest predictor of N 2 O saturation, and its positive association with N 2 O intensified under acidic conditions according to linear mixed models. In the same model, ammonium, dissolved organic carbon, and stream depth also showed significant but weaker positive relationships with N 2 O. Spatial differences among streams explained considerably more variation than seasonal or regional patterns, underscoring the dominance of local factors. Streams with pH 6 consistently exhibited higher N 2 O saturation, and generalized additive modelling indicated a marked decline in N 2 O levels beginning near pH 6. Despite generally high N 2 O saturation, approximately 9 % of observations displayed undersaturation, which occurred mainly in streams with low NO3- concentrations and across all seasons. Our results indicate that acidic, weakly buffered catchments may enhance in-stream N 2 O accumulation even at moderate nitrogen levels. These findings highlight the need to consider pH-related controls when assessing N 2 O dynamics in freshwater networks and when designing mitigation strategies for agricultural landscapes.

articles.title: The open uncertainty window in ocean biogeochemical responses to fossil carbon emissions
articles.titleEn: The open uncertainty window in ocean biogeochemical responses to fossil carbon emissions
articles.abstract: Automated parameter optimisation can effectively reduce model-data mismatch and provide information about ocean biogeochemistry parameter sensitivities, but to what extent it reduces uncertainty in responses to climate change is not well understood. To explore the robustness of simulated ocean biogeochemical responses to a “business-as-usual” RCP 8.5-equivalent fossil CO 2 emission scenario until year 2300, six biogeochemical parameters are optimised against contemporary oxygen, phosphate, and nitrate fields in three different physical configurations of the UVic ESCM. The phytoplankton maximum growth rate parameter value and the nitrogen-to-oxygen molar ratio of organic matter remineralisation were found to be robust across the calibration ensemble, with the former varying less than 1.6 % across the calibrated ensemble and the latter varying less than 4 %. While each calibrated model performs nearly equivalently in terms of optimal total misfit (a result of the model calibration objective), significant differences in biogeochemical fluxes and rates (e.g., global net primary and particulate organic carbon; POC) remain. Application of CO 2 emissions to the calibrated models to the year 2300 produces model responses that start diverging in global average trends in the early 2000s. Models with more sluggish pre-industrial circulations respond less to climate warming in terms of physical changes, but more in their primary production (as these models have been tuned to have weaker limitation on production). Models that have larger changes in circulation metrics due to anthropogenic CO 2 emissions, in particular the Southern Ocean overturning, demonstrate larger changes in shallow (130 m) and deep (2 km) POC fluxes (due to stronger parametric control on particle flux). Suboxic volume trends are smaller in models with larger changes to the physical circulation metrics owing to compensation between model tuning favouring strong biological oxygen consumption in their vigorous pre-industrial state and these models' having a greater physical sensitivity to warming. By the year 2300, the resulting model responses vary by a factor 2.8 in net primary production, 5 in shallow POC fluxes, 1.7 in deep POC fluxes, 1.5 in nitrogen fixation and 1.2 in suboxic volume, but the model spread in absolute values relative to the pre-industrial remains largely unchanged, demonstrating the utility of constraining the pre-industrial ocean state in diverse model ensembles for robust projections of ocean change. However, an uncertainty window remains open in ocean biogeochemical responses to CO 2 emissions, despite systematic tuning.

articles.title: Residual error modelling for process-based flood frequency analysis
articles.titleEn: Residual error modelling for process-based flood frequency analysis
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Flood frequency analysis (FFA) is essential for flood risk management and infrastructure design, yet estimates of flood quantiles remain strongly influenced by the length and representativeness of available streamflow record. We introduce UQ-flood, a process-based flood-frequency framework that integrates a stochastic weather generator, a process-based hydrologic model, and a residual error model developed at the annual-maximum scale. The framework explicitly addresses the presence of errors in simulated annual flood peaks generated by models calibrated to continuous streamflow data. We apply UQ-flood to three Canadian watersheds with contrasting hydroclimatic conditions using 30 years of meteorological and streamflow observations. Long-record empirical annual-maximum estimates provide the primary benchmark, while Bayesian Generalized Extreme Value estimates based on short and long records provide secondary statistical benchmarks for the central flood-quantile estimates. Across the three watersheds, the central UQ-flood estimates remained within the confidence intervals for the long-record discharge quantiles, although their relative proximity to the empirical estimates varied by watershed and return period. Process-based simulations without residual-error correction systematically underestimated flood magnitudes, whereas applying the residual error model shifted the estimated flood-frequency curves toward the long-record observational benchmarks. The framework also propagates residual predictive variability directly at the annual-maximum scale. These results demonstrate that annual-maximum residual error modelling can correct for systematic discrepancies in process-based flood estimates and support central flood-quantile estimation even at sites with short data records.

articles.title: The 2025 Mediterranean marine heatwaves through sea surface temperature analogues
articles.titleEn: The 2025 Mediterranean marine heatwaves through sea surface temperature analogues
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: The Mediterranean Sea experienced an exceptional marine heatwave throughout June–July 2025. Here we analyse this event using an analogue framework that differs from the common atmospheric circulation-based analogue attribution approach. Instead of identifying atmospheric circulation analogues first, we search directly for historical analogues of the observed sea surface temperature (SST) anomaly pattern of the 20 to 30 June 2025 build-up and peak phase, and then compare the associated atmospheric and air-sea surface conditions in a past (1950 to 1986) and a present (1987 to 2024) period, using ERA5 daily fields over the Mediterranean between June and September. Our results suggest that the present period exhibits higher SST anomalies than the past one, with the strongest positive differences over the western Mediterranean and the Adriatic Sea. Warmer 2 m air temperatures over surrounding land areas and higher net shortwave radiation over large parts of the basin are also observed, while sea level pressure, wind speed, latent heat flux, sensible heat flux, and longwave radiation display smaller and more spatially heterogeneous changes. Thus, the 2025 event occurred in a warmer thermodynamic background than analogous SST patterns in earlier decades. Since the analogue framework cannot fully separate externally forced trends from internal variability and it does not explicitly resolve ocean dynamical processes, these results do not constitute a complete formal attribution on their own. Nevertheless, the analogue analysis supports the interpretation that long term warming contributed substantially to the intensity of the 2025 Mediterranean marine heatwave and shows how SST analogue comparisons can complement existing attribution approaches for marine extremes.

articles.title: Multi-data source based quantifying urban flood severity in major Chinese cities (2000–2024) using a hybrid machine-learning weighting framework
articles.titleEn: Multi-data source based quantifying urban flood severity in major Chinese cities (2000–2024) using a hybrid machine-learning weighting framework
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Urban flooding poses a critical challenge to sustainable urban development, yet long-term comparative assessments remain limited by fragmented and heterogeneous disaster records. To address this gap, this study integrates multi-source flood-event data from 20 major Chinese cities during 2000–2024 and develops an impact-based framework for assessing urban flood severity. Official statistics, news reports, and social media records are combined to construct an event-level flood database, which supports the development of a Flood Severity Index (FSI). A hybrid weighting framework that combines conventional weighting schemes with machine-learning-assisted indicator attribution is developed to improve the robustness and interpretability of severity assessment. The results reveal pronounced spatial heterogeneity: southern cities exhibit higher average severity levels and more frequent high-severity events, whereas northern cities generally show lower baseline severity but remain vulnerable to episodic extreme flood impacts. Temporal analysis indicates substantial interannual variability rather than a consistent long-term increasing or decreasing trend. These findings highlight the need for region-specific flood management strategies, including reducing persistent high-severity impacts in southern cities and improving preparedness for abrupt extreme events in northern cities. This study demonstrates the value of integrating fragmented historical records into a comparable framework for urban flood severity assessment.

articles.title: Transient absorption signatures of asymmetric carrier cooling in semiconductors
articles.titleEn: Transient absorption signatures of asymmetric carrier cooling in semiconductors
articles.abstract: Carrier dynamics in semiconductors is central to devices for electronics, optoelectronics, energy, and quantum technologies. Following photoexcitation, electrons and holes relax on ultrafast timescales, yet resolving their individual dynamics remains challenging because widely used pump-probe spectroscopies, such as transient absorption (TA), probe the combined carrier response. Here, we disentangle the cooling dynamics of excited electrons and holes through a joint experiment-theory approach that combines high time-resolution femtosecond TA spectroscopy with quantitative first-principles simulations. We show a pronounced asymmetry in electron and hole cooling in both wurtzite and zinc-blende semiconductors, exemplified by gallium nitride (GaN) and gallium arsenide (GaAs). Guided by theory, we unravel signatures of electron and hole cooling in our femtosecond-resolved TA spectra and show that the TA response is dominated by electron cooling, which occurs on characteristic timescales on the order of 100 fs and is governed by scattering with optical phonons. In contrast, our simulations predict that hole cooling is one order of magnitude faster and produces a comparatively weak contribution to the TA response. Our study reveals the microscopic origin of this asymmetric carrier cooling, establishing it as a general feature of direct-gap wurtzite and zinc-blende semiconductors. Our work shows a predictive experiment-theory framework for understanding the individual dynamics of excited electron and hole carriers, with broad implications for conventional and quantum materials.
