articles.title: Depressed chemical weathering inhibited climate stabilization after the end-Permian biocrisis
articles.titleEn: Depressed chemical weathering inhibited climate stabilization after the end-Permian biocrisis
articles.abstract: The Permian-Triassic transition (∼252 million years ago) marks the most severe mass extinction in Earth’s history, followed by a protracted interval of environmental instability and delayed biological recovery. Although elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) from extensive volcanism is widely invoked, the role of continental weathering feedbacks in regulating global climate has not been effectively constrained. Here, we present high-resolution lithium isotope records from marine carbonates and terrestrial deposits through the Permian-Triassic transition. Combined with an Earth-system model, our data reveal notable decreases in global continental weatherability following the end-Permian mass extinction, inferred to associations with widespread deforestation (extinction of deep-rooted plants) and the collapse of terrestrial ecosystem. This diminished weathering response to volcanic carbon emissions likely contributed to prolonged high atmospheric CO 2 and global temperature during the Early Triassic. The sustained greenhouse conditions, in turn, inhibited contemporaneous marine and terrestrial ecosystem recoveries. Our findings highlight the importance of terrestrial ecosystem in modulating global carbon cycle stability, and its effects on Earth’s habitability.

Combined with an Earth-system model, our data reveal notable decreases in global continental weatherability following the end-Permian mass extinction, inferred to associations with widespread deforestation (extinction of deep-rooted plants) and the collapse of terrestrial ecosystem. This diminished weathering response to volcanic carbon emissions likely contributed to prolonged high atmospheric CO 2 and global temperature during the Early Triassic. articles.title: Dams not to blame for all reservoir carbon emissions from retained organic carbon
articles.titleEn: Dams not to blame for all reservoir carbon emissions from retained organic carbon
articles.abstract: Dams trap organic carbon (OC) and create carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) and methane (CH 4 ) emission hotspots within reservoirs, underlying the ongoing debate over their role in carbon emissions. However, even without dams, this labile OC would still decompose and emit CO 2 or CH 4 during downstream transport and after deposition in estuaries. Thus, relying solely on dammed reservoir observations to assess these emissions may introduce considerable bias. Here, we simulated both dammed and non-dammed scenarios for 5346 global reservoir dams to assess their impact on carbon emissions from retained OC. The results show that reservoir-only approaches overestimate dam-induced carbon emissions by neglecting baseline emissions under no-dam conditions. After baseline correction, dams increase carbon emissions by an average of 21.5% in CO 2 -equivalent (CO 2 -eq), which represents only 18.6% of the emissions estimated using the conventional reservoir-based accounting approach. XGBoost identified reservoir depth and hydraulic residence time as the primary controls on dam-induced carbon emissions.

articles.title: Hyperlocal sensing and inverse modeling reveal community impacts of urban air pollutant emissions
articles.titleEn: Hyperlocal sensing and inverse modeling reveal community impacts of urban air pollutant emissions
articles.abstract: Addressing urban air pollution requires identifying, quantifying, and mitigating emission sources, yet bottom-up inventories often lack fine spatiotemporal precision and rarely capture unpermitted or informally operated sources. We combine dense mobile and fixed-site measurements in a Bayesian inverse modeling framework to produce hourly, hyperlocal black carbon (BC) emission maps (150 meters by 150 meters) that reveal how and where key sources are underrepresented. In West Oakland, CA—an overburdened community near major freight infrastructure—our approach identifies underestimated and unaccounted emission sources, increasing estimated BC emissions by ∼33%. These corrections quadruple the contribution of neighborhood and port-related sources to population-weighted exposures (from 5 to 20%), disproportionately affecting low-income neighborhoods adjacent to freight corridors. Our results demonstrate that combining dense observational data with inverse modeling enables detection and quantification of overlooked emissions, supporting targeted intervention. Sensitivity analyses indicate similar performance with a substantially reduced fixed-site network (∼10 monitors; ∼1 site per square kilometer, compared with 6.7 sites per square kilometer in the full campaign), paired with time-averaged mobile maps, supporting applicability in data-limited urban settings.

articles.title: Engineering bacterial morphology through MreB remodeling enhances one-carbon metabolism for sustainable bioproduction
articles.titleEn: Engineering bacterial morphology through MreB remodeling enhances one-carbon metabolism for sustainable bioproduction
articles.abstract: The actin-like cytoskeletal protein MreB controls bacterial cell morphology, yet whether engineered modulation of MreB-associated architecture can improve microbial metabolism remains largely unexplored. Here, we established a chemical-genetic platform in Escherichia coli combining an engineered MreB variant (A53R) that remodels cellular morphology with A22-mediated perturbation of MreB dynamics. MreB(A53R) reshaped cell morphology and engaged an RpoE-Cra-GadE regulatory network associated with cellular adaptation, which remodeled electron transport, redirected carbon flux toward NADPH-generating pathways, and reduced intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS). Consequently, engineered strains exhibited enhanced formaldehyde tolerance and efficient assimilation of methanol and other C1 substrates. Acute A22 treatment recapitulated the morphological alteration but failed to induce metabolic rewiring, revealing a two-stage adaptive response involving immediate physical adaptation associated with cell envelope reinforcement and long-term transcription-dependent metabolic adaptation to persistent morphological remodeling. The analogous V45R mutation in the native methylotroph Bacillus methanolicus partially recapitulated the improved C1 utilization phenotype, supporting the transferability of MreB-based morphological engineering. Collectively, these findings establish MreB-mediated morphological engineering as a strategy to couple cellular architecture with central carbon and redox metabolism and provide a framework for engineering robust microbial chassis for C1 bioconversion.

articles.title: Human hair–bearing skin organoids reveal cell type–specific susceptibility and innate immune responses to herpes simplex virus 1
articles.titleEn: Human hair–bearing skin organoids reveal cell type–specific susceptibility and innate immune responses to herpes simplex virus 1
articles.abstract: Epithelial surfaces are the primary sites of lytic herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) infection following initial exposure or reactivation from latency. To model this complex environment, we used human hair–bearing skin organoids and combined single-cell spatial transcriptomics with imaging to map viral spread and host responses across skin architecture. Our data suggest delayed progression of the HSV-1 life cycle in epidermal keratinocytes and hair follicle cells compared to the dermis. Infection triggered spatially organized host responses, including induction of IER3 in papillary fibroblasts. In basal keratinocytes, IRF3 was up-regulated in both infected and neighboring uninfected cells, consistent with paracrine activation of antiviral signaling. Inflammatory responses were compartmentalized in a cell type–specific manner, with TNFSF9 (4-1BBL) induced in papillary fibroblasts and tumor necrosis factor–α (TNF-α) induced in keratinocytes. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays confirmed secretion of these cytokines and the TNF-α–responsive chemokines CXCL2 and CXCL10. CXCL2 expression was enriched in cells adjacent to TNF-α–expressing cells, highlighting spatial coordination of inflammatory signaling. While interferon-β reduced viral replication, TNF-α and 4-1BBL did not, suggesting that their primary role is to orchestrate immune cell recruitment and activation. These findings establish human hair–bearing skin organoids as a physiologically relevant model for investigating spatial host–HSV-1 interactions.

articles.title: Monsoon zonal seesaw: Development of the South Asian monsoon aridified North Africa in the Cenozoic
articles.titleEn: Monsoon zonal seesaw: Development of the South Asian monsoon aridified North Africa in the Cenozoic
articles.abstract: North Africa experienced a pronounced transition from humid to arid conditions during the early Cenozoic. Meanwhile, the South Asian monsoon underwent substantial intensification, largely driven by the uplift of the Himalayan-Tibetan Plateau. Here, we demonstrate that the two events, which greatly shaped the paleoenvironment and modern regional climate, are not independent responses to paleogeography changes; rather, the former is primarily driven by the latter through the monsoon-desert mechanism, in which South Asian monsoon diabatic heating produces large-scale subsidence and aridity over North Africa. Using multiple ensembles of paleoclimate simulations and a model for the atmospheric response to imposed diabatic heating, we show that the intensification and poleward shift of Asian monsoon rainfall each make comparable contributions to the aridification of North Africa. Our findings identify a persistent dynamical pathway linking the South Asian and North African monsoons and suggest that it played a major role in early Cenozoic North African aridification, while its climatic expression at other times depended on the relative strengths of competing forcings.

articles.title: Coupled carbonate-shale thallium isotopes reveal the evolution of deep-marine anoxia during the end-Permian mass extinction
articles.titleEn: Coupled carbonate-shale thallium isotopes reveal the evolution of deep-marine anoxia during the end-Permian mass extinction
articles.abstract: Ocean anoxia played a key role in the end-Permian mass extinction, the most severe biotic crisis in Earth’s history, yet reconstructions of oxygenation through this event have lacked a focus on deep-water oxygen loss. Thallium isotopes, which track deep-ocean oxygenation via manganese oxide burial, offer a potential solution but have only been applied to siliciclastic sections, limiting spatial and temporal coverage. Here, we present a combined carbonate-shale Tl isotope record, spanning four geographically distant regions and providing a near-continuous record of global-scale redox change during the extinction interval. Both lithologies record deep-marine anoxia beginning 1 million years before the extinction, demonstrating that carbonate- and shale-hosted Tl isotopes preserve consistent redox signals. Late Permian oxygen depletion likely remained largely constrained to the deep ocean and was distinct from the shelf- and slope-depth euxinia of the Early Triassic that was coupled with climate warming and central to the loss of animal diversity.

articles.title: ANME-2a perform methane oxidation in brackish coastal sediments via multiple pathways
articles.titleEn: ANME-2a perform methane oxidation in brackish coastal sediments via multiple pathways
articles.abstract: Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas. Typically, a large fraction of methane formed in coastal sediments is removed via anaerobic oxidation of methane (AOM). Here, we demonstrate the potential for a range of AOM pathways in brackish coastal sediments by ANME-2a archaea. At our study site, geochemical profiles indicate that AOM is primarily restricted to a shallow, metal oxide–rich sulfate-methane transition zone (SMTZ). ANME-2a were the sole methanotrophs detected, and metatranscriptomics showed the highest expression levels of the ANME-2a genes in the SMTZ. AOM activity was observed in sediment incubations with various electron acceptors, including sulfate, metal oxides, and the organic matter analog graphene oxide. Highest potential rates were observed in sediments from below the SMTZ, pointing toward fast stimulation of the deeper methanotrophic community when alleviating the electron acceptor limitation. The variety of AOM pathways and persistence of methanotrophs below the SMTZ likely contribute to the resilience of the microbial methane filter in brackish coastal sediments.

articles.title: More Frequent, Faster, and Seasonally Reorganized Drought‐to‐Pluvial Transitions in U.S. Cities
articles.titleEn: More Frequent, Faster, and Seasonally Reorganized Drought‐to‐Pluvial Transitions in U.S. Cities
articles.abstract: Hydroclimatic variability is projected to intensify under continued warming, yet the evolving likelihood, rapidness, and seasonal timing of drought‐to‐pluvial transitions remain poorly quantified. Here, we develop a probabilistic framework that integrates a severity‐resolved Markov formulation to estimate conditional drought‐to‐pluvial transition probabilities, Event Coincidence Analysis to quantify Relief Time (TR; the interval between drought amelioration and subsequent pluvial onset), and circular statistics to characterize the seasonal timing of post‐drought pluvial occurrence. We apply this framework to the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index derived from a 20‐member ensemble of downscaled climate‐model projections for 27 U.S. cities representing all nine National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Climate Regions. Results reveal a systematic reorganization of drought‐to‐pluvial dynamics under future warming. For severe drought thresholds, drought‐to‐pluvial transitions increase by approximately 132%–154%, while severe drought states increase by 128%–203% relative to historical conditions. Across most cities, Relief Time shortens by 0.1–0.3 months, indicating increasingly abrupt transitions from drought to wet conditions. Seasonal timing also reorganizes, with the first post‐drought pluvial event shifting by approximately 1–3 months in many regions. Joint changes in transition probability and TR reveal distinct regional acceleration regimes characterized by increasing transition frequency, increasing abruptness, or both. The findings indicate that future drought recovery may increasingly occur through faster, more frequent, and seasonally altered transitions to wet conditions. The proposed framework provides transferable metrics for diagnosing drought‐to‐pluvial behavior and offers actionable insights for flood‐risk assessment, water‐resource management, and climate adaptation under a warming climate.

articles.title: SLAMS‐2.0: A Stochastic, Lagrangian Particle‐Resolving Modeling Framework for Investigating the Biological Carbon Pump
articles.titleEn: SLAMS‐2.0: A Stochastic, Lagrangian Particle‐Resolving Modeling Framework for Investigating the Biological Carbon Pump
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Sinking biogenic particles drive the ocean biological carbon pump (BCP), yet the processes governing their formation, transformation, and fate remain poorly constrained and are difficult to represent with existing modeling frameworks. Traditional approaches either resolve particle populations as bulk distributions or simulate individual particles at high computational cost, limiting their ability to capture both particle‐scale processes and emergent particulate fluxes. Here we present SLAMS‐2.0, a stochastic, particle‐resolving Lagrangian framework that bridges particle‐based and population‐based approaches by explicitly simulating individual, heterogeneous particles and their probabilistic interactions while efficiently capturing the evolving particle population across the full size spectrum through a “superparticle” formulation. The model combines this approach with observation‐informed BCP process representations, allowing particle composition, microstructure, and interactions to emerge dynamically from first‐principles fractal scaling and stochastic encounter dynamics. SLAMS‐2.0 is evaluated at six open‐ocean time‐series sites spanning contrasting biogeographical regimes against a wide range of observations, including particulate organic carbon (POC) and biogenic mineral fluxes, particle abundances, and size distributions. We show that carbon packaging, porosity, mineral ballast, and aggregation efficiency—rather than particle size or sinking velocity alone—govern POC flux transfer to depth, with large, porous, ballast‐rich aggregates driving deep‐ocean POC flux. SLAMS‐2.0 provides a framework for investigating how particle physicochemical attributes and interactions shape emergent carbon fluxes, with applications to both observational process studies and the development of improved biogeochemical model representations.

articles.title: Pervasive patterns in bird songs resemble those in human speech and song and are independent of vocal learning
articles.titleEn: Pervasive patterns in bird songs resemble those in human speech and song and are independent of vocal learning
articles.abstract: Bird songs are often described as analogs to human speech and songs, but expansive comparisons are necessary to determine analogy and mechanistic substrates. By analyzing global corpora consisting of 367 bird species (>74,500 vocal elements from ~5900 songs) within two clades of vocal learners (oscines and hummingbirds) and related nonlearners (suboscines and nightjars) and 52 human languages (>15,000 elements in >800 speech or song phrases), we revealed common patterns in bird songs that resemble prevalent patterns in human speech and song with variation in resemblance to speech or song. Vocal learning did not systematically affect acoustic patterning or similarity to human vocalizations. These data underscore the deep analogies between bird and human vocalizations and convergent motor mechanisms shaping communication.

articles.title: The global geography of threats to freshwater biodiversity
articles.titleEn: The global geography of threats to freshwater biodiversity
articles.abstract: Human activities are eroding biodiversity, especially in freshwater systems. Despite major advances in quantifying species vulnerability and threats, we still lack a crucial understanding of where threats are affecting freshwater species globally. Here, we produced a species-centered spatial assessment of threats, mapping the impact of 45 threats across 21,490 freshwater species of amphibians, fish, mammals, odonates, and reptiles. We found that species in highly developed and water-managed regions are strongly affected by multiple overlapping threats. Although threats vary across taxa and regions, increasing threat probabilities elevate extinction risk and population declines, with freshwater species experiencing greater threat intensity and distinct spatial patterns than terrestrial species. Our findings establish a spatially explicit baseline for targeting the most urgently needed freshwater conservation and management interventions.

articles.title: Intrinsic gestational timing governs human cerebellar development after preterm birth
articles.titleEn: Intrinsic gestational timing governs human cerebellar development after preterm birth
articles.abstract: Intrinsic programs shape brain maturation; however, which of these programs are perturbed by prematurity as well as the molecular pathways involved remain unknown. The human cerebellum serves as a paradigm of extrauterine development—its accelerated growth and circuit formation align with the third trimester, a period disrupted by preterm delivery. Using multimodal datasets encompassing in vivo neuroimaging and neurodevelopmental outcomes with postmortem spatial-transcriptomic and histopathological profiling, we show that prematurity diverts the cerebellar developmental trajectory. Cerebellar growth and functional outcomes scaled with gestational age, despite modifying perinatal exposures. Spatially resolved developmental programs underlying macroscopic trajectories were marked by incomplete granule cell maturation and impaired Purkinje cell structural refinement, which indicate lineage-specific developmental asynchrony. Thus, prematurity constitutes biologically displaced maturation, in which infants of equivalent postmenstrual age occupy divergent developmental states.

articles.title: Data-driven discovery and rapid, direct synthesis of MXenes
articles.titleEn: Data-driven discovery and rapid, direct synthesis of MXenes
articles.abstract: MXenes are a rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides, yet scalable synthesis routes remain limited and historical reports suggest a broader, largely unexplored chemical space. We used machine learning–assisted database mining to uncover hidden multilayer MXenes. Screening reveals 33 previously synthesized but unrecognized MXene candidates. Guided by these findings, we synthesized seven multilayer MXenes using a rapid, scalable self-propagating high-temperature method that requires no sustained external heating and completes within minutes. We further realized 11 previously unexplored rare earth–based MXenes (M = praseodymium, neodymium, samarium, gadolinium, terbium, holmium, and thulium). Experiments and modeling suggest semiconducting behavior and diverse magnetic states across this family. Together, these results expand the MXene family and demonstrate a data-driven strategy for accelerating materials discovery through sustainable methods.

articles.title: Genomic erosion across avifauna in a biodiversity hotspot sounds a conservation alarm
articles.titleEn: Genomic erosion across avifauna in a biodiversity hotspot sounds a conservation alarm
articles.abstract: Loss of biodiversity can have a hidden dimension—the cryptic erosion of genetic diversity even in the face of apparent species resilience. We quantified changes in genetic diversity by comparing historical and modern genomes of 62 songbird species from the Gaoligong Mountains, a biodiversity hotspot in southwestern China. We identified genomic loss averaging between 43 and 49%; and, unexpectedly, common species were disproportionately affected. We argue that this loss was driven primarily by habitat fragmentation (and mitigated by dispersal ability) and show that it exceeds prior estimates and conservation policy thresholds. Species identified as having lost diversity continue to be listed as “Least Concern” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List of Threatened Species, exposing a blind spot in extinction risk monitoring. We call for genomic metrics to be rapidly integrated into global conservation frameworks.

articles.title: When AI takes away the thrill of discovery
articles.titleEn: When AI takes away the thrill of discovery
articles.abstract: “Pure math is being devastated or revolutionized, depending on your point of view.” So said Cornell professor Steven Strogatz after the artificial intelligence (AI) company OpenAI announced in early September a potential solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems that represent the highest goals for mathematical proofs. OpenAI’s solution involved unleashing an army of AI agents at a cost of millions of dollars in computing power, and it also certainly drew on decades of human effort in mathematics before it. Then a few weeks later, OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts describing progress on 372 mathematical problem families, and Google DeepMind published (in Science ) solutions from their own AI math system. These events are potentially exciting for those who long to know the answers to these problems as soon as possible, but they have also sent the world of mathematics reeling, and pose an even bigger question for all fields: Can the satisfaction of understanding ever replace the thrill of discovery?

articles.title: High-resolution mapping of pluvial flooding in ungauged agricultural catchments
articles.titleEn: High-resolution mapping of pluvial flooding in ungauged agricultural catchments
articles.abstract: Accurate pluvial flood mapping in ungauged agricultural catchments is often constrained by a lack of calibration data. This study evaluates a parsimonious, high-resolution (1 m) distributed framework assessing peak discharge along concentrated flow paths, validated against 39 events recorded at two nested outlets (84 and 111 ha) of a single experimental catchment. The framework decouples the rainfall-runoff process to systematically compare adjusted Soil Conservation Service Curve Number (SCS-CN) formulations against two spatially explicit routing algorithms (SCS velocity method vs. Simulator for Water Resources in Rural Basins, SWRRB). Within this specific local context, findings demonstrate that the Jain initial abstraction method significantly reduces volumetric bias, with the distributed approach statistically outperforming lumped modelling. However, performance remains strictly regime-dependent, driven by rainfall intensity rather than total depth. This exposes the structural limits of static Curve Number (CN) parameterizations in capturing rapid Hortonian dynamics, causing the model to dampen minor events while amplifying high-intensity storms. Regarding hydraulic transfer, both routing strategies yield statistically equivalent performance (median Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) values of 0.35 vs. 0.34). Crucially, while the routing phase acts as a mechanical propagator of volumetric uncertainty, it effectively synchronizes the overall runoff window. Applied to 25- and 100-year design storms, this framework illustrates hydrodynamic attenuation and kinematic synchronization at confluences. While primarily validated on a single well-monitored catchment, these findings illustrate the approach's potential to pinpoint hydraulic hotspots, with initial benchmarks indicating promising scalability to larger agricultural landscapes.

articles.title: Enhancing hydrological representation of the Brahmaputra basin through terrestrial water storage and surface soil moisture Data Assimilation
articles.titleEn: Enhancing hydrological representation of the Brahmaputra basin through terrestrial water storage and surface soil moisture Data Assimilation
articles.abstract: Understanding the dynamics of terrestrial water storage (TWS), and its components such as surface soil moisture (SSM) and groundwater, is important for the Brahmaputra River basin, where water resources are expected to experience increasing demand and are highly vulnerable to extreme hydrological events and climate change. However, water storage dynamics are complex and difficult to capture by state-of-the-art large-scale hydrological models. In this study, we implement a multi-variate daily TWS and daily SSM sequential Data Assimilation (DA) to integrate the satellite observations in the World Wide Water Resources Assessment model (W3RA) with the aim of improving model-derived water storage dynamics. In our methodology, we propose a model space covariance localization approach that is compared with three other approaches used in the previous literature. The results show that this new approach is the only one to effectively reduce cross-variable influences along the vertical water storage profile, which have been reported as one of the main challenges of multi-variate land DA. A validation of the multi-variate DA estimates (for the period 2004–2015) indicates that more realistic decadal trend and inter-annual variability are introduced into the TWS and groundwater estimates, increasing the correlation coefficients with the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index and observed groundwater levels by +0.24 to +0.54 correlation points. With respect to SSM, DA induces a general phase shift, especially around mountain areas. Improved land water storage estimates reveal a land water decline of 70.9 GT per decade for the period 2004–2015 in the Brahmaputra River basin, which constitutes approximately half of the TWS decline in that period, with the other half caused by glacier retreat (67.5 GT per decade).

articles.title: EnsAI: an emulator for atmospheric ammonia ensembles
articles.titleEn: EnsAI: an emulator for atmospheric ammonia ensembles
articles.abstract: Ensemble-based methods for data assimilation and emissions inversions are a popular way to encode flow-dependency within the model error covariance. While most ensemble methods do not require the use of an adjoint model, the need to repeatedly run a geophysical model to generate the ensemble can be a significant computational burden. In this paper, we introduce EnsAI , a new AI-based ensemble generation system for surface ammonia concentrations. When trained on an ensemble for ammonia generated by the GEM-MACH air quality model, it was shown that the ensembles produced by EnsAI can accurately reproduce the meteorology-dependent features of the original ensemble, while generating the ensemble 3300 times faster than the original GEM-MACH ensemble. While EnsAI requires an upfront cost for generating the ensemble used for training, as well as the training itself, the long term computational savings can greatly exceed these initial computational costs. When used in an emissions inversion system, EnsAI produced similar inversion results to those in which the original GEM-MACH ensemble was used while using significantly less computational resources.

articles.title: Using a two-stage Rosenbrock solver to increase computational efficiency in the DOE's Exascale Earth System Model version 1 (E3SMv1)
articles.titleEn: Using a two-stage Rosenbrock solver to increase computational efficiency in the DOE's Exascale Earth System Model version 1 (E3SMv1)
articles.abstract: The integration of stiff atmospheric chemical systems is a major computational cost in Earth System Models and poses challenges for numerical stability as chemical complexity and temporal resolution increase. In this study, we implement a semi-implicit two-stage Rosenbrock method (ROS2) in the Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 1 (E3SMv1) and evaluate it as an alternative chemistry time-integration scheme. ROS2 is tested with two interactive chemical mechanisms of substantially different size: chemUCI (60 prognostic species) and trop_strat_mozart_mam4 (155 prognostic species). Numerical experiments include short simulations to quantify computational cost, a box-model timestep-refinement analysis, and one-year integrations to examine numerical stability and solution sensitivity. At the same 180 s chemistry timestep, ROS2 requires approximately 33 % less chemistry integration time than the original iterative implicit solver on the tested Cori/KNL CPU platform. The magnitude of this speedup is configuration dependent. Global-mean surface-ozone differences among the tested configurations are small (≤ 1.03 ppb), and the one-year integrations show no evidence of numerical instability. Spatial and diurnal differences in ozone, NO, NO 2 , and OH are species- and mechanism-dependent, indicating sensitivity to both timestep and solver formulation rather than a common systematic bias. These results support ROS2 as a lower-cost alternative to the current implicit integrator when E3SM chemistry is operated at short timesteps; additional timestep-refinement tests and benchmarking on contemporary CPU/GPU systems are needed to quantify coupled-model convergence and performance portability.

articles.title: The Global Gravity-based Groundwater Product (G3P)
articles.titleEn: The Global Gravity-based Groundwater Product (G3P)
articles.abstract: Groundwater is one of the most important freshwater resources for ecosystems and mankind. Because of its fundamental role in the Earth's water and energy cycles, groundwater has been declared an essential climate variable by GCOS, the Global Climate Observing System. Similar to other subsurface states and fluxes, groundwater is difficult to monitor at the global scale, with sufficient spatial coverage and over climate-relevant time scales. The Global Gravity-based Groundwater Product (G3P) is a global observation-based data set of large-scale groundwater storage variations. G3P capitalizes on the unique capability of GRACE and GRACE-FO satellite gravimetry as the only remote sensing technology to monitor subsurface mass variations. In a mass balance approach, satellite-based, in situ observation-based and model-based water storage variations of snow water equivalent, root-zone soil moisture, glacier mass, and surface water storage are subtracted from GRACE/-FO terrestrial water storage anomalies to result in monthly variations of groundwater storage. For this combination, the individual compartmental storage data are spatially filtered to be consistent with the spatial resolution of terrestrial water storage from satellite gravimetry. The G3P data set presented here covers the period 2002 to 2023 with monthly resolution on a 0.5° global grid and includes propagated uncertainty information. We describe the details of the G3P data processing chain and of each contributing data stream including their uncertainties and limitations, provide examples of spatial and temporal groundwater storage variations represented by the G3P data set, and present exemplary evaluation results against in situ groundwater observations for three large aquifer systems. The latter show moderate to high temporal correlation of aquifer-average G3P groundwater storage and in situ groundwater level variations on seasonal and interannual time scales. G3P is a prototype for an operational global groundwater service, under development as a cross-cutting extension of the existing portfolio of the Copernicus Climate Change Service C3S. The G3P data set is available via GFZ Data Services at https://doi.org/10.5880/g3p.2024.001 (Güntner et al., 2024).

articles.title: A gapless 0.05° daytime-hourly tropospheric NO 2 dataset (2019–2024) over key Asian hotspots reconstructed using physics-aware deep learning
articles.titleEn: A gapless 0.05° daytime-hourly tropospheric NO 2 dataset (2019–2024) over key Asian hotspots reconstructed using physics-aware deep learning
articles.abstract: High-frequency observations of tropospheric nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ) support regional air quality assessment and analysis of its photochemical evolution. Although the Geostationary Environment Monitoring Spectrometer (GEMS) and other new-generation geostationary satellites provide hourly observations during daytime, their spatial coverage is often severely compromised by cloud obstruction and inherent retrieval limitations. Furthermore, their short observation history hinders long-term, cross-regional environmental assessments. To address this, this study presents a gapless, 0.05° daytime-hourly tropospheric NO 2 vertical column density (VCD) dataset for representative hotspots in Asia spanning 2019 to 2024, reconstructed using a physics-aware deep learning framework. The framework integrates partial convolutions to handle irregularly missing satellite observations and proposes a Physics-aware Normalization (PhysNorm) module. Specifically, the model inputs comprise the 0.05° TROPOMI tropospheric NO 2 VCD and its validity mask, together with 0.25° predictors including ERA5 meteorological variables, EAC4 total-column NO 2 , land cover, elevation, and the cosine of the solar zenith angle. The supervised training target is the hourly GEMS tropospheric NO 2 VCD from 2023. PhysNorm dynamically modulates 0.05° high-resolution feature maps using 0.25° low-resolution physical features, thereby ensuring rigorous physical continuity while filling data gaps. Validation results show that the model performs exceptionally on the test set ( R 2 = 0.889) and maintains high generalization stability in an independent validation on 2024 data, which was not used for training. Cross-validation against an independent polar-orbiting satellite instrument (GOME-2C) confirms the reliability of the dataset in reconstructing pollution hotspots and its applicability to periods without GEMS observations (2019–2022). Comparison with independent ground-based Pandora observations showed an overall correlation of R =0.644 for 2019–2024. Using this reconstructed dataset, this study finely delineates the periodic diurnal characteristics of NO 2 in typical Asian regions and characterizes inter-annual variations in NO 2 concentration patterns over the past six years. This newly generated dataset provides a spatiotemporally continuous daytime record, overcoming the limitations of cloud cover and short observational histories, thereby facilitating long-term, high-resolution air quality assessments and epidemiological studies. This dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20427767 (Gao et al., 2026).

articles.title: A global eddy-collocated temperature and salinity profile dataset (v1.0): integrating multiplatform in situ observations with satellite-tracking mesoscale eddies
articles.titleEn: A global eddy-collocated temperature and salinity profile dataset (v1.0): integrating multiplatform in situ observations with satellite-tracking mesoscale eddies
articles.abstract: Mesoscale eddies are ubiquitous rotating water masses with horizontal scales of tens to hundreds of kilometers that play a key role in redistributing heat and salt throughout the global ocean. However, the lack of long-term observational records has limited systematic assessments of their thermohaline effects from regional to global scales. Here, we present a global eddy-collocated temperature and salinity profile dataset spanning 29 years (1993–2021), constructed by integrating multiplatform in situ hydrographic observations with satellite-derived mesoscale eddy tracking products. The dataset contains 5.46 million quality-controlled temperature–salinity profiles, each collocated with its nearest mesoscale eddy and is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20607854 (He, 2026). The observations provide broad global coverage, with most 2° × 2° grid boxes containing more than 200 profiles, enabling statistically robust analyses of eddy-induced temperature and salinity anomalies. Validation against previously documented regional eddy signatures demonstrates that the dataset reliably captures characteristic temperature and salinity anomaly structures associated with eddies. Example applications demonstrate its utility for characterizing regional three-dimensional eddy thermohaline patterns, assessing global eddy effects on upper ocean stratification and subsurface temperature extremes, and providing an observational basis for estimating eddy-induced heat, salt, and water-mass transports. As a long-term observation-based eddy-collocated profile product, this dataset provides a valuable resource for studies of eddy impacts on ocean circulation, tracer redistribution, climate variability, and model evaluation.

articles.title: Ise Bay Reanalysis (IBRA): a 12-year ecological hydrodynamic reanalysis dataset for Ise Bay, Japan
articles.titleEn: Ise Bay Reanalysis (IBRA): a 12-year ecological hydrodynamic reanalysis dataset for Ise Bay, Japan
articles.abstract: Reanalysis datasets based on coupled ocean circulation and ecosystem models are essential tools for understanding coastal environmental variability and supporting water-quality management. However, the development of such datasets for semi-enclosed coastal systems remains limited, particularly for those incorporating subsurface biogeochemical observations such as dissolved oxygen (DO). This study presents the Ise Bay Reanalysis (IBRA), a high-resolution, 12-year (2011–2022) reanalysis dataset of hydrodynamic and biogeochemical variables for Ise Bay, Japan. The dataset was generated using the Ecological hydrodynamics simulation system of the Port and Airport Research Institute Simulator (EcoPARI-Simulator), coupled with an ensemble Kalman filter data assimilation system that assimilated in situ observations of water temperature, salinity, and bottom-layer DO at 6 h intervals. The resulting dataset has an hourly temporal resolution and resolves the entire water column. IBRA has three key distinguishing features. First, unlike many previous reanalysis datasets that rely primarily on satellite observations, IBRA assimilates continuous in situ measurements throughout the water column, including high-frequency DO observations, thereby improving the representation of subsurface dynamics. Second, the 6 h assimilation cycle enables the dataset to resolve short-term variability driven by tidal processes, which are a dominant control of coastal transport and mixing. Third, spatially coherent corrections are applied across the entire bay using an ensemble Kalman filter, ensuring spatial consistency in both physical and biogeochemical fields while avoiding artificial discontinuities often associated with simpler data assimilation approaches. The quality of IBRA was evaluated using statistical metrics and detailed comparisons against in situ observations. Data assimilation improved overall agreement with observations across multiple stations and depths, particularly for bottom-layer DO concentrations. The dataset successfully reproduced seasonal variability, vertical stratification, and the formation and persistence of hypoxic conditions in the inner bay, while also capturing well-oxygenated conditions near the bay mouth. Furthermore, the spatial distributions of temperature, salinity, and DO were realistically represented, including the intrusion of offshore water masses and associated horizontal gradients. The IBRA dataset therefore provides a dynamically consistent and comprehensive representation of physical and biogeochemical variability in a semi-enclosed coastal system. It is expected to serve as a valuable resource for studies of coastal hypoxia, water-quality assessment, and environmental management. The IBRA dataset is publicly available via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19808667 (Matsuzaki et al., 2026).

articles.title: Extreme precipitation events: a comprehensive catalog for northern Chile (17.5° S to 30.0° S)
articles.titleEn: Extreme precipitation events: a comprehensive catalog for northern Chile (17.5° S to 30.0° S)
articles.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive catalog of the most extreme seasonal rainfall events of northern Chile between 1979 and 2019. We analyzed its meteorological patterns across three latitudinal bands (17.5–23.5° S, 23.5–27° S, and 27–30° S) using daily precipitation and mean daily temperature from the CR2METv2.5 product, and vertically integrated water vapor transport data (IVT) from the ERA5 reanalysis. These events were classified into three main precipitation categories: Stratiform , Coast , and Andes Mountain . The Andes Mountain category was further subdivided into five subcategories based on IVT patterns and precipitation spatial distribution: North Andes , South Andes , Along Andes , Convergence , and Westerly IVT . In total, the catalog comprises 472 extreme precipitation events corresponding to 408 unique storm dates, each characterized by date, precipitation category, maximum precipitation within the latitudinal band, average storm temperature, and snow line elevation determined through empirical methods and remote sensing from daily MODIS imagery. The dataset is available as a CSV catalog with additional NetCDF files containing gridded precipitation, IVT, and MODIS snow cover fields for each event. To test the applicability of this catalog, we characterized extreme events composite results for the Austral summer between 27–30° S (latitudinal band 3), showing that events within each category yield coherent synoptic patterns. Additionally, we contrasted our catalog with an existing national landslide inventory of 548 events in the study area, finding that just six cataloged storms (all classified as Stratiform ) account for 203 debris flow events (37 %), indicating the March 2015 and May 2017 storms were alone responsible for 168 of them. We also estimated the approximate debris flow volumes for the March 2015 Atacama event using a transport-capacity approach, showing reasonable agreement for deposits larger than 4000 m 3 . These findings enhance our understanding of extreme precipitation events in Chile and provide a valuable resource for storyline analysis and precipitation pattern identification. Catalog is available at Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/ZENODO.14342935 (Matus et al., 2026).

In total, the catalog comprises 472 extreme precipitation events corresponding to 408 unique storm dates, each characterized by date, precipitation category, maximum precipitation within the latitudinal band, average storm temperature, and snow line elevation determined through empirical methods and remote sensing from daily MODIS imagery. The dataset is available as a CSV catalog with additional NetCDF files containing gridded precipitation, IVT, and MODIS snow cover fields for each event. To test the applicability of this catalog, we characterized extreme events composite results for the Austral summer between 27–30° S (latitudinal band 3), showing that events within each category yield coherent synoptic patterns. Additionally, we contrasted our catalog with an existing national landslide inventory of 548 events in the study area, finding that just six cataloged storms (all classified as Stratiform ) account for 203 debris flow events (37 %), indicating the March 2015 and May 2017 storms were alone responsible for 168 of them. We also estimated the approximate debris flow volumes for the March 2015 Atacama event using a transport-capacity approach, showing reasonable agreement for deposits larger than 4000 m 3 . These findings enhance our understanding of extreme precipitation events in Chile and provide a valuable resource for storyline analysis and precipitation pattern identification. articles.title: Global Change Is Reshaping Coral Communities and Threatening Reef Physical Functionality
articles.titleEn: Global Change Is Reshaping Coral Communities and Threatening Reef Physical Functionality
articles.abstract: Coral reefs are undergoing profound compositional changes driven by climate change, disease, and chronic human disturbance. Coral cover is the primary metric used to track reef condition, but it often fails to capture the contributions of different coral species to reef carbonate production, structural complexity, and associated biodiversity. Here, I review evidence showing that global change disproportionately removes competitively dominant and architecturally complex corals, driving non‐random changes and coral community homogenisation. These changes erode reef functionality, even when overall cover is maintained. Species‐specific contributions to calcification and structural complexity span orders of magnitude, such that targeted losses of framework‐building taxa collapse carbonate budgets and habitat architecture in ways not predictable from cover trends. These structural changes cascade through associated communities, undermining functional diversity and the ecosystem processes on which reef resilience depends. Critically, rebounds in coral cover frequently reflect the colonisation by fast‐growing opportunistic species, which yield slow or absent recovery of physical functionality, while reassembly and the re‐establishment of large, structurally complex colonies (and the physical functionality they provide) might lag by decades. Furthermore, as mass disturbance events occur at ever‐shorter intervals, recovery windows close before reef‐building potential and complexity can be fully restored. Monitoring, management, and restoration should therefore focus on trait‐ and species‐explicit assessments that prioritise protection and restoration of keystone reef‐builders, target sites with high functional potential, and reduce stressors at appropriate scales. Integrating functional metrics into policy and restoration planning is essential to safeguard reef geomorphic and ecological services under continued global change.

articles.title: Shell hash promotes growth in Pacific littleneck clams ( Leukoma staminea ) by altering pore water chemistry
articles.titleEn: Shell hash promotes growth in Pacific littleneck clams ( Leukoma staminea ) by altering pore water chemistry
articles.abstract: Bivalves that build calcium carbonate skeletons are at risk from ocean acidification, and mitigation strategies may be needed to keep coastal populations healthy. It can be energetically costly for organisms like clams and mussels to build their shells under low pH conditions, and acidification can lead to shell dissolution. Adding crushed shells (shell hash) to beach sediments, a practice used by some Indigenous communities and aquaculturists, may mitigate the negative effects of ocean acidification by altering the chemistry of the pore fluids in which they live. We tested the hypothesis that mixing shell hash into the sediment improves the growth and physiology of infaunal Pacific littleneck clams ( Leukoma staminea ). Juvenile clams were raised for 90 d under four conditions: control seawater with sediment, acidified seawater with sediment, control seawater with sediment plus shell hash, and acidified seawater with sediment plus shell hash. Pore water and overlying seawater were sampled three times a week for pH, alkalinity, salinity, temperature, and dissolved oxygen. Clam shell weight, soft tissue weight, and new shell growth were measured, and mantle tissue RNA was collected for gene sequencing after three months. Our results demonstrate that the addition of shell hash increased the pH of pore water relative to the control, acidified water decreased animal growth, and the presence of shell hash partially mitigated the effect. Gene expression profiling suggests that animals in acidified seawater with shell hash were largely indistinguishable from animals in non-acidified water. Our experimental results suggest that adding shell hash to sediments alters the chemistry of pore fluids, buffering against acidic conditions that can negatively affect the growth of economically and culturally important shellfish like littleneck clams.

articles.title: Contribution of fine roots on carbon allocation patterns in Norwegian forests
articles.titleEn: Contribution of fine roots on carbon allocation patterns in Norwegian forests
articles.abstract: Boreal forests play a key role in the global carbon (C) cycle, with fine root production and turnover contributing to belowground C fluxes and inputs to soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks. However, fine root biomass and production are difficult to quantify and introduce uncertainty in estimates of net primary production (NPP), limiting the assessment of C allocation patterns in boreal forests. The objective of the present study was to assess how different fine root modelling approaches influence estimates of NPP, gross primary production (GPP), carbon use efficiency (CUE), and belowground C allocation to fine roots in Norwegian boreal and nemo-boreal forests. Using Norway's national forest resource map together with MODIS remote sensing data, we estimated fine root biomass and production using three approaches that differed in how foliage biomass was derived: two based on leaf area index (from MODIS or the forest resource map) and one based on allometric biomass equations. These approaches were combined with alternative fine root turnover rates and fine-root-to-foliage biomass ratios. Mean NPP derived from the forest resource map ranged from 318 to 243 g C m −2 yr −1 across young to mature forests. In Norway spruce and Scots pine forests, NPP increased during early stand development, peaked between 50 and 80 years, and declined with increasing age. Comparison against European MODIS NPP revealed that tree growth alone accounted for 16 % of MODIS NPP, while including fine root and understory NPP contributions increased total NPP by roughly 3–5 times, depending on the fine root estimation method. CUE ranged from 0.63 to 0.37, showing age-related declines and species-level variation, with the highest values in deciduous forests and the lowest values in Norway spruce forests. Our analysis sheds light on the role of fine root biomass and production in forest C budgeting and their influence on NPP, CUE, and belowground C allocation. Excluding fine roots creates a major gap in forest C analyses and we conclude that the choice of method for fine root estimation has a strong impact on regional NPP and its component fluxes. Estimates of forest CUE may guide management by identifying areas with low efficiency, where interventions may enhance forest C uptake.

articles.title: Impacts of shrub coverage for arctic ecosystem carbon uptake and storage
articles.titleEn: Impacts of shrub coverage for arctic ecosystem carbon uptake and storage
articles.abstract: Although shrubs employ different water and carbon-use strategies compared to trees and are expanding rapidly across warming tundra and grassland, they are not adequately represented in global land surface models. In this study, we incorporated two types of shrubs, deciduous and evergreen, into the QUINCY nutrient-enabled terrestrial biosphere model, which features a state-of-the-art treatment of soil nutrient dynamics and carbon exchange. We investigated changes in carbon (C) fluxes and storage due to shrub cover, it's response to climate and CO 2 fertilization effect, as well as the role of nitrogen availability. With this new implementation, shrubs exhibited reasonable seasonal cycle of gross primary production (GPP) at 50 % of the Arctic study sites. The model achieved mean R 2 values of 0.5 on average, when compared with field measurements and remote sensing products, which represents an improvement for evergreen shrubs compared with the old model parametrization. However, the model-measurement agreement is lower at sites with heterogeneous local vegetation, which is not captured by the model hydrology or represented by the shrub plant functional type. The modelled gross primary production of shrubs is similarly distributed compared to needleleaf evergreen forest, with no significant difference in the median. Compared to graminoids, shrubs' carbon fluxes are 40 % higher. Shrubs produce substantial above-ground biomass, albeit lower than needleleaf trees, and exhibit distinct phenological patterns. While CO 2 fertilization generally benefits all plant types, shrubs appear to have particularly robust growth under elevated CO 2 concentrations. Providing the plants with unlimited nitrogen doubled gross primary production at most sites and improved the model-measurement agreement by 15 % whereas the modelled deciduous shrubs substantially reduce their nitrogen sources more than evergreen shrubs. A similar effect occurred when nitrogen and carbon contents were initialized based on permafrost profiles, which partly alleviated nitrogen limitation in the model. Overall, this study demonstrates the impact of evergreen and deciduous shrub vegetation on the Arctic carbon cycle and ongoing changes. It recommends including shrub plant functional types in global Earth system models. However, the strong nitrogen limitation of Arctic shrub productivity when using standard model parameterizations suggests that global models underestimate the Arctic's contribution to global land carbon.

articles.title: Global socio-economic resilience to disasters
articles.titleEn: Global socio-economic resilience to disasters
articles.abstract: Most disaster risk assessments use asset damages as their central metric, often neglecting distributional impacts and affected people’s coping and recovery capacity. To address this, the concepts of well-being losses and socio-economic resilience—the ability to experience asset damages without a decline in well-being—have been proposed. Here we provide a global picture of well-being losses and socio-economic resilience using microsimulations. Across 132 countries, 1 dollar in damages causes well-being losses equivalent to a 2-dollar uniform national consumption drop. The poorest populations incur only 9% of damages but 33% of well-being losses. A 10% higher gross domestic product per capita is associated with a 1 percentage point resilience increase. Low-income countries experience 72% greater well-being losses per dollar of damages and need 92% longer to recover than high-income countries. Socio-economic and financial interventions can complement asset-focused policies, and targeting low-income populations usually yields higher well-being returns. Our results offer a starting point for a discussion on more comprehensive risk metrics and risk management policies for sustainable development.

articles.title: An Investigation of the Characteristics of Indian Summer Monsoon Low‐Pressure Systems Under Stratospheric Aerosol Geoengineering
articles.titleEn: An Investigation of the Characteristics of Indian Summer Monsoon Low‐Pressure Systems Under Stratospheric Aerosol Geoengineering
articles.abstract: Monsoon Low‐Pressure Systems (LPSs) that govern the rainfall of the Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) contribute more than half of its rainfall and extreme rainfall events. In this study, we explore how LPS activity changes under greenhouse warming and Stratospheric Aerosol Intervention (SAI) using simulations from the fully coupled CESM2.1.3 climate model. We simulate three different climate scenarios: CTRL (control climate), 2XCO2 (doubling of ), and UNIFORM (a globally uniform stratospheric sulfate aerosol forcing superimposed on the 2XCO2 climate). In the 2XCO2 simulation, the global mean surface temperature increases by 3.22 K, accompanied by a weakened ISM circulation, reflected in a weaker Walker circulation, reduced vertical zonal wind shear, and weaker low‐level Barotropic Shear (BS). However, despite 6% increase in the All‐India rainfall (AIR) due to increased atmospheric water vapor, the total count of LPSs and LPS days decreases by approximately 9%–14%, but the systems on average produce stronger rainfall and extreme rainfall events in central and northern India. The UNIFORM scenario restores global mean surface temperature within 0.03 K of CTRL and partially revives monsoon circulation, BS, and recovers LPS frequency and spatial distribution toward CTRL levels. However, this aerosol experiment forcing suppresses the hydrological cycle, decreasing atmospheric moisture and AIR by 3.82% compared to CTRL (9.28% relative to 2XCO2), along with weakened LPS rainfall and extreme rainfall events. In summary, while uniform SAI can partially revive monsoon circulation and LPS activity, it simultaneously suppresses the thermodynamically driven increase in rainfall and extreme rainfall events associated with greenhouse warming.

articles.title: Vegetation increasingly controlled by atmospheric dryness rather than soil moisture
articles.titleEn: Vegetation increasingly controlled by atmospheric dryness rather than soil moisture
articles.abstract: Terrestrial vegetation regulates global carbon cycling and climate through responses to water availability. Yet, it remains unclear whether soil moisture (SM) or atmospheric dryness (vapour pressure deficit, VPD) dominates vegetation responses and, more critically, how their relative influence changes over time, limiting predictions of ecosystem–climate feedback under warming. Here we analyse satellite-derived vegetation variability over the past four decades using an explainable artificial intelligence framework that disentangles nonlinear hydroclimatic driver contributions. We show SM dominates vegetation variability in most regions. However, VPD influence has strengthened while SM influence has weakened over time. These changes highlight an asymmetric transition with more SM-dominated ecosystems shifting towards increasing VPD control than vice versa. Changes in the mean and variability of SM and VPD drive this transition by altering plant water-stress responses. Continued warming will probably intensify this pattern as rising VPD and more frequent extreme events strengthen atmospheric constraints on vegetation.

articles.title: OceanTracker 0.5: fast adaptable Lagrangian particle tracking in structured and unstructured grids
articles.titleEn: OceanTracker 0.5: fast adaptable Lagrangian particle tracking in structured and unstructured grids
articles.abstract: Particle tracking is frequently used to compute particle movements within hydrodynamic ocean models; however, modelling millions of particles is computationally challenging. OceanTracker is designed to reduce the time required to obtain results from particle tracking. Firstly, OceanTracker is computationally efficient, allowing users to simulate large numbers of particles in complex coastal environments, enabling improved statistics and exploration of a wider range of cases within acceptable run times. Secondly, OceanTracker can calculate multiple particle statistics during the computational run, eliminating the need to record and post-process large volumes of particle trajectories. The adaptability of OceanTracker's modular computational pipeline allows users to add and modify components that govern particle physics, behaviour, and statistics. The computational pipeline is entirely assembled from user-provided parameters, supplied as a JSON or YMAL text file or built using helper methods. Coders can easily modify existing components through code inheritance. Currently, OceanTracker supports hydrodynamic model output both for unstructured (SCHISM, FVCOM, DELFT3D-FM) and structured (ROMS, NEMO/GLORYS) grids. Computing the trajectories for more than one million particles with OceanTracker on a single computer core is more than ten times faster than the OpenDrift code and twice as fast as the Parcels code, despite treating structured grids as unstructured, which might be expected to be computationally slower than structured grids due to the time required to locate each particle within a hydrodynamic grid cell. In addition to its single-core performance, OceanTracker can run computations in parallel across available cores. This can further increase speed by up to an order of magnitude on currently available multicore desktop processors.

articles.title: Calibration guidelines and a runoff-isotope module for lake proxy system modeling (PRYSM v2.0)
articles.titleEn: Calibration guidelines and a runoff-isotope module for lake proxy system modeling (PRYSM v2.0)
articles.abstract: Lake sediments preserve information about past air temperature and precipitation, providing critical, real-world targets to validate climate models. However, these paleoclimate data encode information about multiple climate signals as well as lake dynamics, which makes comparison of paleoclimate data and model output challenging. Proxy system models (PSMs), or forward models that translate climate variables into proxy units, are tools for mechanistically interpreting paleoclimate data. PRYSM v2.0 is a PSM for paleoclimate data archived in lake sediments. Foundational to the accuracy of the PSM is a comprehensive understanding of the modern lake system supported by observations and meteorological inputs. However, two obstacles exist. First, stable oxygen and hydrogen isotope values in lake water are the target of many proxies preserved in lake sediments, but the PSM does not have a built-in catchment model to aid simulation of isotope values. Additionally, calibration of uncertain model parameters requires observations and expert knowledge of the lake system, yet most sites are unmonitored. Here, we advance PSMs for lake sediment archives by integrating a simple runoff-isotope module that can be adapted to any lake and reproduce the seasonal timing and magnitude of two mid-latitude lakes with contrasting morphometry, hydrology, and mixing regimes. Using multi-year observational datasets from the lakes, we conduct model experiments that require the PSM to predict the temperature and δ 2 H values of lake water when calibrated to a single observed profile, which mimics common observation collection challenges. For these lakes, observations from the warm, ice-free season are most informative and constrain uncertain parameter values that best generalize to unseen data from other water depths and years. Our framework for running and calibrating the PSM is available as open-source tools in Python, aiding the application of this PSM to the vast global database of lake sediment paleoclimate time series.

articles.title: On combining climate models into weighted ensembles
articles.titleEn: On combining climate models into weighted ensembles
articles.abstract: Several methods have been proposed and used to refine estimates of future climate change based on combined output from comprehensive climate models. While previously the so-called model democracy approach was used to combine model outputs, where every model is given equal weight, it is now widely accepted that using model weights that account for model performance and model independence is necessary to obtain more reliable results. However, most existing approaches rely, implicitly or explicitly, on a similar statistical basis, while describing things in different ways. Here we distinguish between approaches that are based on the performance of individual models (individual performance weighting) and approaches that are based on the performance of the weighted ensemble as a whole (ensemble performance weighting). At the same time, we formulate both in probabilistic Bayesian terms to make their application and comparison straightforward. Using simple constructed examples, we demonstrate that the ensemble performance weighting approach implicitly accounts for co-dependencies among models, which arguably makes the computation of independence weights for the purpose of model weighting obsolete. We also show that a set of weighted models within the ensemble weighting approach will naturally tend to artificially reduce uncertainty and that this is strongly influenced by the choice of the prior distribution over weight vectors. The distinction between individual and ensemble performance weighting is both methodological and conceptual. Formulating both approaches in general probabilistic Bayesian terms as done here, can serve as a common basis for future developments with regard to ensemble model weighting in Earth system science. The discussed concepts are generally applicable across domains and are thus possibly relevant for other modeling communities as well.

Formulating both approaches in general probabilistic Bayesian terms as done here, can serve as a common basis for future developments with regard to ensemble model weighting in Earth system science. The discussed concepts are generally applicable across domains and are thus possibly relevant for other modeling communities as well.

articles.title: Liquid polymer enhances methanogenesis and restructures prokaryotic communities in freshwater sediments
articles.titleEn: Liquid polymer enhances methanogenesis and restructures prokaryotic communities in freshwater sediments
articles.abstract: The widespread use of synthetic hydrophilic polymers, such as polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP), has raised concerns about their potential effects on environmental biogeochemical processes, yet their impact on sediment ecosystems remains largely unexplored. We investigated how PVP influences methane (CH 4 ) production and prokaryotic community composition in freshwater sediments over a 56 d anoxic incubation. PVP exposure accelerated the onset of methanogenesis, increased maximum CH 4 production rates, and elevated maximum CH 4 concentrations. Notably, a substantial proportion of the response occurred already at environmentally relevant concentrations. These functional changes were accompanied by shifts in bacterial communities, particularly among fermentative taxa known to produce key methanogenic substrates. In contrast, archaeal communities, including methanogens, exhibited comparatively weak and transient responses. The concomitant increase in CO 2 and CH 4 production and the observed microbial community shifts suggest that PVP altered microbial carbon-processing pathways, although the mechanisms responsible for these effects remain unresolved. As a proof-of-concept study, our results provide initial evidence that a widespread synthetic hydrophilic polymer can modify sediment microbial communities and stimulate methane production. These findings highlight the need for future studies addressing the mechanistic basis of these responses and their relevance under environmentally realistic conditions.

articles.title: Synthesis of greenhouse gas emission factors for forest organic soils in the Köppen–Geiger Dfb climate zone
articles.titleEn: Synthesis of greenhouse gas emission factors for forest organic soils in the Köppen–Geiger Dfb climate zone
articles.abstract: Greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from organic soils are a key component of land-use-related emissions, particularly in countries with large areas of organic soils. Temperate-zone forest soils remain less studied in GHG research than boreal soils. However, recent work has expanded coverage in the northeastern temperate region, which, under the Köppen–Geiger climate classification, shares key climatic characteristics with the southern boreal region (Dfb). This study synthesised updated GHG flux data to evaluate carbon balance and emissions from forest organic soils in the Dfb zone, stratified by drainage status, nutrient availability, and dominant tree species. Such stratification revealed CO 2 source-sink patterns, which encourage the ecological relevance of using these categories for data aggregation. The dominant tree species reflected nutrient status: drained coniferous and deciduous stands have been reported as CO 2 sources, emitting 0.03 ± 0.55 and 0.47 ± 0.29 t CO 2 -C ha −1 yr −1 , respectively, though soils tended to shift toward CO 2 sinks in stands older than 25 years. In contrast, undrained soils have generally been observed to function as CO 2 sinks, although not necessarily in all sites. However, this stratification was less informative for CH 4 and N 2 O. CH 4 fluxes were primarily determined by water table level rather than by other site variables, whereas N 2 O showed a tendency toward elevated emissions in deciduous stands, irrespective of drainage status.

articles.title: Carbonation of silicate minerals contributes to atmospheric CO2 drawdown in glacier-fed streams
articles.titleEn: Carbonation of silicate minerals contributes to atmospheric CO2 drawdown in glacier-fed streams
articles.abstract: Glaciers produce abundant grains of reactive minerals that influence inorganic carbon cycling, yet the links between mineral weathering and CO 2 dynamics in glacier-fed streams (GFSs) remain poorly understood. Here we combine streamwater geochemistry, solute end-member modelling, carbonate saturation calculations and suspended-sediment mineralogy across 170 GFSs worldwide. We show that 69% of GFSs were undersaturated with respect to atmospheric CO 2 equilibrium, indicating widespread atmospheric CO 2 uptake. Grain-scale analyses of selected carbonate-bearing GFSs reveal metastable Mg-bearing carbonate phases consistent with secondary mineral formation in transient microenvironments. We propose that CO 2 released during sulfuric acid-driven carbonate weathering and secondary calcite precipitation can be partly consumed by carbonation of silicate- and clay-derived mineral surfaces, transferring dissolved inorganic carbon into particulate inorganic carbon. This sediment-mediated pathway can contribute to CO 2 undersaturation under favourable lithological and geochemical conditions, revealing a previously underappreciated coupling between chemical weathering, sediment–water interactions and inorganic carbon storage in proglacial landscapes rapidly expanding under global glacier retreat.

articles.title: Satellite‐Based Assessment Reveals Patterns of Coastal Marsh Carbon Sequestration Along the U.S. East and Gulf Coasts
articles.titleEn: Satellite‐Based Assessment Reveals Patterns of Coastal Marsh Carbon Sequestration Along the U.S. East and Gulf Coasts
articles.abstract: Coastal marshes are critical blue‐carbon ecosystems, yet regional quantification of vegetation‐derived carbon burial and living biomass carbon stocks within marshes remains limited. Here, we developed a transparent, measurement‐based framework integrating Sentinel‐2 data (2019–2024), field biomass measurements, marsh‐type distribution maps, and literature‐derived marsh‐type‐specific carbon allocation parameters to estimate living biomass carbon stocks and vegetation‐derived burial rates across tidal marshes of the U.S. East and Gulf Coasts. Among tested vegetation indices (VIs), the Green Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (GNDVI) showed the strongest relationship with field‐measured above‐ground biomass (AGB) across seasons and marsh types. Applying the calibrated GNDVI–AGB relationship, we mapped annual peak AGB and used seasonal AGB differences as a satellite proxy for net above‐ground primary production (NAPP). By combining remotely sensed AGB with marsh‐type‐specific allocation strategies, vegetation carbon fractions, and below‐ground burial efficiency, we quantified regional living biomass carbon stocks and vegetation‐derived carbon burial rates. Our results suggest, along the East and Gulf Coasts, mean living biomass carbon of about 832 ± 202 g C m −2 , corresponding to a total of 11.1 Tg C, and a mean vegetation‐derived carbon burial rate of 70 ± 47 g C m −2 yr −1 , totaling about 0.94 Tg C yr −1 . These vegetation‐derived burial rates are comparable to those of seagrass meadows and mangrove forests, demonstrating that coastal marshes function as similarly effective blue‐carbon sinks despite differences in plant structure and productivity. This study demonstrates that remote sensing provides a transparent, scalable, and cost‐effective approach for monitoring blue‐carbon dynamics and informing coastal management strategies.

articles.title: Spatiotemporal Propagation and Future Risks of Agricultural Drought in Response to Meteorological Drought Across Asia
articles.titleEn: Spatiotemporal Propagation and Future Risks of Agricultural Drought in Response to Meteorological Drought Across Asia
articles.abstract: Under the background of global warming, drought risk has intensified. Clarifying the changing patterns and response relationships of different drought types is vital for risk management and climate change adaptation. Using multi‐model data from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase VI (CMIP6) and an improved three‐dimensional clustering algorithm, this study identified meteorological and Agricultural drought (AD) events in Asia. We analyzed the spatiotemporal differentiation, migration patterns, and response relationships between the two drought types under different future Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs). The results showed that, under the historical scenario, AD events outnumbered Meteorological drought (MD) events by 77 occurrences, while their average duration was 0.2 months shorter than that of meteorological droughts. The spatiotemporal correlation between meteorological and AD varied regionally, being strongest in Central Asia and southern East Asia, while weak or negative in North Asia and the Qinghai‐Tibet Plateau. Under future scenarios, from SSP1‐2.6 to SSP5‐8.5 scenario, meteorological droughts exhibited longer duration, and both types showed higher severity. The average duration of MD events increased from 2.3 to 3.9 months, and the average migration distance extended from 1,166.3 km to 2,650.4 km. The proportion of matched pairs in which MD preceded AD rose from 29% under SSP1‐2.6% to 60% under SSP5‐8.5. Under the scenarios of SSP2‐4.5, SSP3‐7.0 and SSP5‐8.5, a model‐derived crossover between the fitted SPEI and SSMI trends occurs around 2058. These findings reveal the complex and transitive nature of future drought risk in Asia and provide a scientific basis for formulating targeted drought‐resistance strategies.

articles.title: Imminent Emergence of Permanent Surface Marine Heatwave States Across Global Oceans
articles.titleEn: Imminent Emergence of Permanent Surface Marine Heatwave States Across Global Oceans
articles.abstract: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) can devastate ocean ecosystems, yet the timing at which anthropogenic changes in MHW characteristics permanently emerge from natural variability at the global scale remains poorly quantified. Here, we present the first global time of emergence analysis of MHW characteristics of the ocean surface using simulations from 21 Earth system models from the sixth Coupled Model Intercomparison Project under moderate (SSP2‐4.5) and high (SSP5‐8.5) greenhouse gas emissions scenarios. Relative to a 1985–2014 baseline, we find that almost 48% of the global ocean has already experienced significant trends in both annual MHW days and frequency. Across tropical oceans, MHW conditions permanently emerge between 2020 and 2040 regardless of emission pathway, indicating that near‐term transformation is unavoidable. By mid‐century, half the global ocean is projected to experience MHW conditions for at least 50% of the year, increasing to 90% by 2100. Regions experiencing the strongest warming show the earliest emergence, with uncertainty in emergence timing comparatively low in the tropics (10–15 years) but expanding substantially at higher latitudes (30 years). These findings demonstrate that persistent, large‐scale marine thermal stress is imminent, demanding transformation from reactive crisis management to anticipatory ocean governance within the next two decades.

articles.title: A single-molecule spin–photon interface
articles.titleEn: A single-molecule spin–photon interface
articles.abstract: Optical interfaces that connect long-lived spin qubits to photons are a central requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum information processing. At present, solid-state atomic defects are leading candidates because of their inherent spin and optical coherence 1,2 . Building on these advancements, synthetically tailored molecular systems represent a fundamental change in the field, using precise atomic control and consistent bottom-up assembly 3,4 . However, a molecular platform that concurrently satisfies the demands of a robust spin–photon interface—namely, the combination of bright fluorescence, high spectral stability and long ground-state spin lifetimes—has yet to be realized at the single-molecule level. Here we show that a triplet ground-state carbene molecule, embedded within a structurally matched host crystal, functions as a robust spin–photon interface with single-molecule addressability. The system exhibits narrow ZPLs, spectral stability over more than an hour, spin-selective optical transitions and single-molecule optically detected magnetic resonance. Coherent control yields millisecond-scale dynamical-decoupling coherence and tens-of-milliseconds spin relaxation at a temperature of 4.5 K. These results establish molecular qubits as a viable platform for single-emitter quantum optics 5,6 while preserving the advantages of bottom-up chemical design 7 and processable materials 8–10 .
